title: Introduction to Special Census
content:
Special Census Overview

What is the Special Census (SC) Program?

The purpose of the Special Census program is to enumerate the population and housing units at the request of your local government. Many states use special census population statistics to determine the distribution of state funds to local jurisdictions. Local jurisdictions may use the data to plan new schools, transportation systems, housing programs, or water treatment facilities. A Special Census is a basic enumeration of population, housing units (HUs), group quarters (GQ), and transitory locations (TL) conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau in the years between Decennial censuses; every 10 years, the national census, known as the Decennial Census. Local residents are hired and trained to conduct the Special Census. They are conducted on a cost-reimbursable basis. For Special Census purposes, a governmental unit is defined as the government of any state, county, city, or other political subdivision within a state, or the government of the District of Columbia or the government of any possession or area including political subdivisions, American Indian Reservations, or Alaskan Native villages. During a Special Census, Field Representatives (FRs) visit assigned areas and canvass, that is, travel systematically all streets, roads, and paths in the assigned area, to find all living quarters. While canvassing, they verify or update the Census Bureau's address lists, based on what they observe on the ground and through interviews with respondents. At each address identified as a housing unit, FRs interview an occupant and complete a Special Census questionnaire for the household. To measure the quality of the work performed, the Special Census program includes several quality control (QC) checks. Field Supervisors (FSs) review FR work progress. A separate team of FSs and FRs performs QC checks on completed assignments, which includes dependent quality checks and reinterviews.

title: Why the Special Census Program Conducted
content:
The purpose of the Special Census program is to give governmental units an opportunity to conduct a census for their community in the years between Decennial Censuses. Receiving up-to-date census information about their communities helps local and tribal governments to:
  • Be eligible for receiving increased state funds and grants for schools, hospitals, roads, public works, and other vital programs.
  • Improve the ability to plan for schools and better transportation.
  • Improve public safety and emergency preparedness.

title: Where is the Special Census Program Conducted?
content: A Special Census may be taken wherever a governmental unit determines it is beneficial: in counties, neighborhoods, governmental units, or other geographic areas in the United States and Puerto Rico.

title: What is the Special Census Date?
content:
The U.S. Census Bureau and the local government will determine a reference date for collecting the data. This date is called the *Special Census Day*.
It is critical that all data collected are based on the status of the address on the Special Census Day.

title: The U.S. Census Bureau
content:
## The Role of the U.S. Census Bureau
The Special Census program is conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau - the federal government's largest statistical agency.
As the leading source of quality data about the nation's people and economy, the Census Bureau honors privacy, protects confidentiality, shares our expertise globally, and conducts our work openly. The Census Bureau is guided on this mission by our strong and capable workforce, our readiness to innovate, and our abiding commitment to our customers.
The primary function of the Census Bureau is to conduct, every 10 years, the national census, known as the Decennial Census. The primary reason for conducting the Decennial Census is to determine the number of seats in the U.S. House of Representatives each state will have, based on its population. But there are many other reasons why the Decennial Census and other censuses, including Special Censuses, are important.
- Responses to the 2020 Census shape how more than \$675 billion in federal funding is distributed annually to local communities.
- Responses determines further political representation in Congress.
- Population totals and breakdowns by sex, age, race, and other factors inform decisions about distribution of Federal funds, grants and support to states, counties, and communities.
- Governments and businesses use Census results to plan new investments, services, and jobs.
- Developers use census data to build new homes and revitalize old neighborhoods.
- Local governments use census data for public safety and emergency preparedness.
- Residents use census data to support community initiatives involving legislation, quality-of-life, and consumer advocacy.
- The census has always been a record of our history. The 2020 Census will shape a roadmap for our future.
Refer to Appendix A to learn about other surveys the Census Bureau may be conducting at regular or irregular intervals in the Special Census enumeration areas.

title: Who's Who in the Special Census
content:
## Overview
A Special Census has positions at the Special Census Office (SCO) and in the field. The following sections provide a concise summary of various job positions and their respective responsibilities
Your role in the office is crucial for the success of the Special Census and it ensures the collection of high-quality data.

title: Structure of the Census Bureau Staff
content: Conducting a Special Census is an involved process that takes many people to maintain.

title: Census Bureau Headquarters
content: The U.S. Census Bureau Headquarters in Suitland, MD developed the Special Census program, including training materials and procedures used by Regional Offices (RO), Special Census Office (SCO), and field staff. Census Bureau Headquarters oversees the ROs.

title: Regional Office (RO)
content:
ROs are permanent offices that coordinate and carry out survey and census field data collection operations for the Census Bureau and its customers. ROs oversee the SCOs. The ROs are:
**New York (RO# 2200).** Located in New York, NY, the NYRO serves Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, and Vermont.
**Philadelphia (RO# 2300).** Located in Philadelphia, PA, the PHRO serves Delaware, District of Columbia, Kentucky, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia.
**Chicago (RO# 2500).** Located in Chicago, IL, the CHRO serves Arkansas, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, and Wisconsin.
**Atlanta (RO# 2900).** Located in Atlanta, GA, the ATRO serves Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, and South Carolina.
**Denver (RO# 3100).** Located in Lakewood, CO, the DNRO serves Arizona, Colorado, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, South Dakota, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming.
**Los Angeles (RO# 3200).** Located in Burbank, CA the LARO serves Alaska, California, Hawaii, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, and Washington.

title: Special Census Office (SCO)
content: SCOs are temporary offices established to conduct the Special Census program.

title: Special Census Supervisor
content:
The Special Census Supervisor (SCS) works under the supervision of the RO Coordinator and manages all activities of the Special Census Office. The Special Census Supervisor performs the duties of the Field Manager (FM) when the Special Census does not hire a FM. The Special Census Office Supervisor:
- Reviews and certifies FR and FS payrolls in GovTA
- Assists with recruiting, at the discretion of the RO, if the governmental unit has not recruited enough applicants to work on the Special Census.
- Oversees clerical operations in the office, including the review of questionnaires and address registers as well as all Quality Control (QC) operations.
- Communicates with the Special Census Manager.
- Promptly responds to messages.
- Directs duties of SCO staff.
- Make final decision on reinterview questionnaire when there is a discrepancy with the original questionnaire.
- Monitors daily progress and performance reports.
- Meets with governmental units to discuss special census operations, office space, timing, publicity, and the status of local-recruiting efforts, when directed by the RO.
- Oversees the use of MOJO to track the flow of work to and from the field. MOJO activities include the check-out/check-in of address registers, the check-in of questionnaires and address registers and the keying of selected data.
- Takes corrective actions, as appropriate, to keep the operation on schedule.
- Transmits completed materials on a timely basis.
- Completes all special census final reports and transmitting them to the RO, HQ, and to governmental units, as appropriate.
- Manages the Special Census Field Managers (FMs).
- Is available for discussions with the FM.
- Performs the duties listed below under FM when the SCO does not hire a FM.

title: Special Census Office Clerks
content:
Special Census clerks perform a variety of tasks in the Special Census Office. The office clerks:
- Prepare address registers (AR) for assignment.
- Checkout work to the Field Supervisors.
- Reassign work to Field Representatives after the FS makes assignments or reassignments.
- Check in completed assignments as work is returned to the SCO.
- Review completed work as it is returned to the SCO.
- Document errors on completed work that is returned to the SCO and return to the FS.
- Prepare Form SC-RQ, Special Census Reinterview Questionnaire, as production questionnaires are selected for Reinterview.
- Conduct telephone Reinterview, as assigned.
- Run daily reports and provide to the SCS and the FM.
- Assist with SCO closeout activities.
- Audit, enter time and validate timesheets for FRs and FSs.

title: Special Census Field Manager (FM)
content:
FMs directly manage Field Supervisors (FS). Each FM oversees approximately 6-8 FSs. FMs train FSs and monitor work assignments and work progress for each FS team. FMs also certify submitted FS payroll records and advise and assist FSs on personnel and performance issues. The FM is the main point of contact for all field activities. The Field Manager:
- Promptly responds to messages.
- Meets with FSs daily to discuss progress of the team's work, discuss performance, or conduct issues, provide guidance on difficult of unusual situations.
- Is available for phone calls from the Field Supervisor.

title: Special Census Field Supervisor (FS)
content: FSs directly supervise Field Representatives (FRs). Each FS oversees a team of approximately 6-8 FRs. FSs train FRs, provide assignments, and monitor FR progress and performance as they conduct their work. FSs discuss FR conduct and performance issues with the FM. FSs also provides feedback on job performance and answer work-related questions.

title: Special Census Field Representative (FR)
content: FRs are responsible for working the Special Census assignments. This work includes traveling to the assigned area, verifying or updating the provided address list, and conducting interviews with respondents to collect data as required for the Special Census.

title: Employee Responsibilities
content:
## Become Familiar with Special Census Materials and Procedures
The SC-1202, Special Census Field Representative (FR) Manual contains specific FR instructions for conducting the Special Census field operation. The SC-1130, Special Census Field Supervisor (FS) Manual contains the specific instructions for supervising FRs in the field and the procedures for the quality assurance activities. The Special Census Supervisor (SCS) must be familiar with these documents to understand the Special Census operation. This manual, the SC-50, Special Census Office Manual, contains specific instructions for office staff.
Depending on the Special Census Office (SCO), Group Quarters (GQ) or Transitory Locations (TL) operations may be implemented in your Special Census area. The SC-569.12, Group Quarters Field Representative Manual and SC-569.30, Transitory Locations Field Representative Manual contain the specific instructions and procedures to conduct these operations in the field. The Special Census Supervisor may need to also be familiar with these documents to understand these operations and its implementation in the field.

title: Title 13
content:
Protection under Title 13 of the U.S. Code guarantees confidentiality of census information and establishes penalties for disclosing this information.
This means that only people sworn to protect Title 13 data may see information the Census Bureau collects. Protected information cannot be shared with anyone who is not sworn to maintain the confidentiality of Title 13 protected data -- including the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internal Revenue Service, or a court of law.
Unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by a sworn Census Bureau employee is punishable by a fine of up to \$250,000, imprisonment of up to 5 years, or both. You must never reveal census information to anyone who is not a sworn Census Bureau employee.

title: Data Stewardship
content:
The Census Bureau workforce is bound to protect confidential information by an ironclad commitment backed by Federal law. Data Stewardship means providing quality data for public good while protecting individual privacy and confidentiality. This is the Census Bureau's core responsibility. We may not release personally identifiable information.
Data Stewardship assures the Census Bureau can effectively collect high quality data to be used by its customers while meeting the legal and reporting obligations of Title 13, the Privacy Act, and other applicable statutes. Keeping the public's trust is critical to our ability to carry out our mission as the leading source of quality data about the nation's people and economy.

title: Ways to Maintain Confidentiality as a Data Steward
content:
Here are ways you can maintain the confidentiality of all census information:
- When not working, always lock your vehicle whenever Special Census materials are in it. Store Special Census materials out of view.
- Do not show the address lists, maps, or completed questionnaires to anyone.
- Be sure no one else can hear you if discussing Title 13 protected data with your manager in public places.
- Do not share personally identifiable information (PII) with another sworn Census Bureau employee who does not have a need to know.
- Always ask your manager if you are not sure whether something is considered personally identifiable information (PII).
Remember that when you took the confidentiality oath, you were sworn for life.

title: The Privacy Act of 1974
content:
The Privacy Act of 1974 requires that each Federal agency advise people of their rights when collecting information from them. Specifically, a person must know under what law the information is being collected, how the information will be used and whether they must answer.
The SC-CN(E/S), Confidentiality Notice, contains the information required by the Privacy Act of 1974. Special Census staff must give a Confidentiality Notice to each person from whom they request census-related information. Never leave this notice at an address where no one is home or that is vacant. It must always be handed to a person.

title: Data Falsification
content:
There may be times when work is not progressing well. Even though you want to do a good job and keep on schedule, you may encounter problems. However, no matter what the circumstances, work must never be falsified. All data collected must be obtained from an occupant, knowledgeable person, or through observation. Never search for information from public records or on the Internet.
Your manager and other office personnel are trained to recognize bogus materials. A percentage of all work is verified for accuracy. The chances of catching falsified data are very high. If it is discovered that someone submitted falsified data, they will be dismissed immediately.
**Anyone willfully falsify information collected under Title 13, United States Code, Section 213, can be found guilty of perjury (fabrication) and may be fined up to \$250,000 and/or imprisoned up to five years. If it is determined that the falsification was intentional, they will be removed from federal service.**

title: Media Contacts While You Are Working
content:
As you go about your work, reporters from local newspapers, radio, or TV stations may approach you seeking an interview. They may even want to accompany you while you work. If this happens:
- Stop work immediately. Walk away from the location where you are working to make sure the address is not identified.
- Do not:
- Allow the reporter(s) to see any of your work materials.
- Let the reporter(s) overhear or observe any meetings or interviews you are conducting.
- Divulge any information that could lead the reporter(s) to identify a person, such as an address or phone number. Title 13 guarantees respondents that all information the Census Bureau collects will be kept confidential.
- Call your manager.

title: Restrictions on the Political Activities of Federal Employees
content: While you are working for the Census Bureau, you are covered by the Hatch Act, which restricts certain political activities of Federal employees. The following are examples of activities allowed and prohibited under the Hatch Act.

title: Activities Allowed by the Hatch Act
content:
Census Bureau employees may participate in the following activities during non-duty hours:
- Register and vote as they choose
- Contribute money to political organizations
- Attend political fund-raising functions
- Attend and be active at political rallies and meetings

title: Activities Prohibited by the Hatch Act
content:
Census Bureau employees are prohibited from:
- Engaging in political activity while on duty
- Engaging in political activity in a government office
- Engaging in political activity while wearing an official ID badge
- Engaging in political activity while using a government vehicle
- Wearing political buttons or other political items while on duty
- Soliciting or receiving political contributions

title: Partisan Political Signs or Stickers
content: Census Bureau employees may display a partisan political sign or sticker (such as a bumper sticker) on a privately-owned (or borrowed) vehicle if the vehicle is not used for official government work. The employee must remove or cover up any such sign or sticker on the vehicle during the period in which the vehicle is used for official government work (for example, while the employee is on duty). Employees may display a partisan political sign or sticker from a past partisan political campaign after the election, so long as the person is not currently running in a partisan political campaign.

title: How Does the Hatch Act Affect You?
content:
Please remember that it is your responsibility to raise any questions or concerns about permissible political activities to your manager. Federal employees should be aware that certain political activities might also constitute criminal offenses under Title 18 of the U.S. Code.
For more information on the Hatch Act, please refer to the SC-590, Census Employee Handbook for Field Representatives.

title: Lost, Missing, or Stolen Materials
content:
As a census employee, you are responsible for protecting all materials assigned to you, including your Census Bureau-issued ID badge. You must take special care to protect Address Registers, labeled questionnaires, completed questionnaires, and other materials containing Title 13 data that are in your possession. These materials must be always accounted for.
You are responsible for:
- Using census-owned property for the sole purpose of conducting official government-related work
- Properly caring for, handling, and protecting the Address Registers, questionnaires, your Census Bureau-issued ID badge, and other materials containing Title 13 data in your possession
- Properly reporting materials that are lost, missing, or stolen [within one hour]{.underline} of the discovery
- Immediately returning all census-owned materials to your manager before transfer, reassignment, or separation from the Census Bureau
Employees may be held financially liable for equipment that is lost, missing, stolen, or damaged due to negligence. The criminal code of the United States also provides penalties for theft, embezzlement, conversion of, or willful damage to government property. Title 18, U.S. Code 641, provides penalties of up to \$250,000 and/or 10 years of imprisonment. The Census Bureau is committed to using any lawful and reasonable means necessary to recover property owned by the Federal government and to ensuring the security of all Title 13 data in an employee's possession.
**If You Experiences Lost, Missing, or Stolen Materials Containing Title 13 Data**
If the materials are found or recovered, you must notify the Census Service Center at 1-877-343-2010, Option #1, to update them on the status.
If you experience lost, missing, or stolen materials, including your Census Bureau-issued ID badge, you must do all the following:
- If the materials were stolen, call the police, making sure to obtain a police report number.
- Call the Census Service Center (CSC) at 1-877-343-2010 and select Option #1 for Cyber Security, Physical Security, and PII Breach Incident Reporting, to report the incident.
- This must be done within one (1) hour of the discovery of the lost, missing, or stolen materials.
- Provide the police report number (if the materials were stolen).
- Obtain a case number from the Census Service Center operator.
- Notify your manager, inform them of the incident, and provide the police report number (if the materials were stolen).
