title: Arranging for a Special Census
content: This chapter provides a general overview of Special Census (SC) preparatory activities. The responsibilities of the governmental unit (GU), Census Bureau Headquarters (HQ) and Regional Office (RO) staff, including the designated Special Census Supervisor (SCS), are discussed below.

title: Overview of Responsibilities
content:
## Introduction
There is a substantial amount of preparatory work completed by HQ and RO staff before Special Census field work starts. The Special Census Supervisor should be familiar with these activities.

title: Special Census Request Overview
content:
The governmental unit seeking a Special Census submits completed a Form SC-900, Special Census Cost Estimate (CE) Request, to HQ. This form is available on the Census Bureau's Special Census website at: <http://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/specialcensus.html>
Direct link to the form: <https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/special-census/sc-900.pdf>
The governmental unit completes the Form SC-900, Special Census Cost Estimate Request, and provides specific information about the area being considered for the Special Census. The governmental unit must also send a letter from the highest elected official for the cost estimate preparation.
Information from the completed Form SC-900, Special Census Cost Estimate Request, along with suggested pay rates, housing unit (HU) and population count estimates, and other pertinent information are forwarded to the RO by HQ staff. The RO:
- Assesses the information.
- Determines the regional office resources needed to conduct the Special Census for the governmental unit.
- Provides any additional information that would be helpful to the HQ staff in the cost estimate preparation.
HQ staff use the information submitted by the governmental unit and the input from the RO to prepare a cost estimate. HQ staff sends the governmental unit a cover letter, the Special Census (SC) cost estimate, and two copies of a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) outlining the Special Census requirements.
If the cost estimate is acceptable to the governmental unit, the appropriate government local official signs and sends the Memorandum of Agreement back to HQ. Once the governmental unit transfers the necessary funds to the Census Bureau as outlined in the Memorandum of Agreement, the activities to conduct the Special Census for the governmental unit begin.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities
content:
GU are responsible for:
- Requesting a Special Census Cost Estimate in writing.
- Signing the MOA and transferring the necessary funds to the Census Bureau (if the terms and cost are acceptable).
- Reviewing and updating census maps of their SC area, including the Boundary and Annexation Survey (BAS) Map and the Special Census Verification Map.
- Supplying office space and equipment for use by Census Bureau staff for the duration of the SC.
- Recruiting local applicants to work on the SC.
- Conducting outreach activities to educate residents and promote cooperation with the SC Field Representatives (FRs).

title: Headquarters Special Census Staff Responsibilities
content:
There are several divisions in the Census Bureau that work together planning and implementing a SC for a GU. HQ will:
- Coordinate the development of the cost estimate for the GU.
- Prepare a CE letter and sending it to the GU.
- Ensure that the initial payment from the GU is received.
- Prepare fund allocation memos and budget documentation for the distribution of funds to participating divisions for preparatory work, geographic support, processing, and field supervision once full payment is received from the GU.
- Prepare project descriptions and operating plans for each SC.
- Monitor the charges to the SC program.
- Prepare and send out a MOA for signature to the requesting local government. The MOA includes the terms that the GU and the Census Bureau agrees to for conducting the SC.
- Prepare the MOA and handle all communication with the governmental unit relative to the MOA, including:
- Reasons a GU may want to conduct a SC
- SC schedule and timing
- Data collection activities
- Special data requirements
- CE procedures
- Develop procedural and training materials.
- Coordinate, approve, and disseminate any changes to procedures.
- Provide technical and procedural support to the RO.
- Coordinate and oversee the work for the data processing and tabulation activities performed in HQ.
- Prepare and send the SC results letter to the GU, state officials, and the RO.

title: Regional Office Responsibilities
content:
The RO is responsible for implementing and monitoring field data collection activities. The RO also ensures that quality and schedule expectations are met. The RO is involved in all aspects of the SC program, from fielding initial questions about the program before a GU embarks on a SC to answering questions about the final counts after a SC is completed. The staff from the RO are extremely important in maintaining a cooperative and productive relationship with the GU throughout the SC. The RO supports the GU from the initial request for a cost estimate until after field operations end.
Additional information about the support provided during each of the phases is provided below.

title: Prior to Receiving a Signed MOA/Cost Estimate
content:
GU may contact the RO for information and guidance regarding a SC. RO staff should refer the GU to HQ to provide this information and guidance at any point *before* the MOA is signed.
If a GU requests a CE, the RO provides information to the HQ staff for completing the CE. This information includes the feasibility of conducting the SC during the requested time frame, the staffing requirements, and other regional cost factors.

title: After a MOA Is Signed but Prior to Field Operations
content:
Once the MOA has been signed, the RO will:
- Explain the SC BAS Map.
- Explain the Special Census Verification Map.
- Prepare a letter to the GU from the Regional Director (RD)outlining the SC requirements and needs. See Appendix E for an example template of this letter.
The letter usually includes information on:
- Requirements for secure office space, equipment, telephone lines, and other requirements.
- SC publicity.
- Staffing requirements.
- Scheduling.
- Designating the Special Census Supervisor (SCS).

title: During Field Operations
content:
The RO support responsibilities during the field operation include:
- Ordering SC supplies from the National Processing Center (NPC).
- Providing technical and procedural support to the SCS.
- Responding to inquiries from HQ staff.
- Monitoring the progress of the SC and reporting ongoing status to SC HQ staff.
- Ensuring all quality assurance procedures are fully and correctly implemented.

title: Post Field Operations
content:
After field operations are over, the RO responsibilities include:
- Ensuring all materials used in the SC are sent to the appropriate destinations. Some materials go to NPC, the RO or HQ. See *Chapter 18: Closing Out the Special Census* for more information about SC materials disposition.
- Closing the Special Census Office (SCO).

title: Working with Governmental Units
content:
## Introduction
It is important that the RO, as well as the Special Census Supervisor, know who the key contact people are in the GUs. The RO and the Special Census Supervisor need to establish and maintain communications with the GUs. The RO has the flexibility to determine the contact frequency and communication method with the GU prior, during, and after the SC.
The communication methods and frequency may vary from RO to RO or from Special Census to Special Census. This section provides some suggestions and guidance for effective interactions and communications with the GUs. The RO will provide the Special Census Supervisor guidance on how to communicate with the GUs.

title: Initial Contact with Local Officials
content:
The RO is responsible for contacting the GU after the MOA has been signed and the required funds for the SC have been transmitted to the Census Bureau. Depending on the location of the SC, the contact may be made via telephone or personal visit. It is suggested that this initial contact should occur to notify the governmental that the Census Bureau received the signed MOA and to confirm the funds were received by the Census Bureau.
The RO should also inform the GU they will receive a letter with information about the requirements and responsibilities of the GU to conduct the SC, and other materials, such as the SC Program, Guidebook for Sponsors.

title: Regional Director's Letter of Governmental Unit Responsibilities
content:
Shortly after a SC MOA has been signed and the required funds are transferred to the Census Bureau, HQ staff notifies the RO that it may start working with the GU.
The RO prepares an initial letter outlining the GUs responsibilities for conducting the SC in their jurisdiction within two weeks of receiving notice from HQ to start working with the GU.
Among the GUs responsibilities are:
- Provisioning of the office space and equipment, such as laptops and printers.
- Recruiting the required number of job applicants.
- Recommending outreach activities to promote resident cooperation and participation.
The letter specifically states:
- The amount of required office space square footage.
- The number of chairs and tables.
- The telephone and internet equipment requirements.
- The number of applicants that must be recruited.
- Other pertinent requirements for conducting a SC.
At least one copy of the SC Program, Guidebook for Sponsors, should be included with the initial Regional Director's letter*.* This allows the GU time to review the guidebook and formulate questions for the initial conversations and/or meetings.
The RDs letter is sent to the highest elected official of the GU. Information contained in this letter may be discussed with the GU at an appropriate or agreed upon time between the RO and the GU.
This discussion may occur when either of the map sets are delivered to the governmental unit for their review, or at the request of the GU. The RO has the discretion to determine at when this discussion should take place.
A letter template is shown in []{.mark}Appendix E.

title: Suggested Agenda when Meeting with the Governmental Unit for the First Time
content:
The GU is likely to have questions after local officials review the SC Program, Guidebook for Sponsors. During the initial contact or visit to the GU, at a minimum, the RO should discuss the following topics with the GU:
- The Census Bureau's point of contact for the GU.
- The purpose for conducting a SC (recent annexations, new housing units, more occupied units, or other reasons).
- The proposed SC schedule, including the SC Date.
- The SC boundaries and the purpose of the Boundary and Annexation Survey Map.
- The purpose of the Verification Map.
- The GU responsibilities, including:
- Supplying office space and equipment, such as laptops and printers.
- Recruiting an adequate number of people for field positions.
- Planning for outreach to residents.
- Planning for publicity to help ensure cooperation.
- Provide and review the SC Program, Guidebook for Sponsors.
- SC operational workflow.
- Conducting quality assurance activities.
- Conducting the SC closeout activities.
Additional information about the discussion topics is provided below.

title: Governmental Unit Point of Contact
content: It is important to document the GUs designated point of contact to ensure effective lines of communication between the local officials and Census staff. Once the GU identifies the designated point of contact person (POC), this is the person through whom all communications regarding the SC should occur.

title: Purpose for Conducting the Special Census
content: The RO staff previously discussed with governmental unit their reasons for requesting a SC. The RO staff (or other designee, which may be the Special Census Supervisor) should also discuss the reasons for the projected increase/decrease of population. This discussion helps ensure that GUs expectations are reasonable. This discussion also provides an opportunity for Census Bureau staff to ask where areas of new housing are located or whether there are other areas within the community that may impact the enumeration process.

title: Proposed Special Census Schedule including the Special Census Date
content:
The RO probes the GU to determine if there are any dates of significance that may impact the results of the SC (e.g., University semester breaks, or migrant populations). The RO must have a general idea of when the GU wants the SC conducted and use the information to accurately schedule the SC.
The Special Census Date is the reference date for all data collection. This includes housing unit status (occupied or vacant) and enumeration status. It is important that the GU be informed of the Special Census Date.

title: Special Census Boundaries and the Boundary and Annexation Survey Map
content:
Depending on the RO's preferences, the first meeting after the MOA has been signed may also be used to deliver and discuss the SC Boundary and Annexation Survey (BAS) Map. The BAS is a Census Bureau program where GUs provide the Census Bureau with updates related to the jurisdiction boundaries and/or annexations. The SC BAS Map contains the most recent jurisdiction boundaries the Census Bureau has for the governmental unit and is used to collect information about the legally defined geographic area to be included in the SC.
A full special census is a basic enumeration of population, HUs, GQs, and at TLs for an area entirely within the jurisdiction of a GU requesting the special census. A partial special census is conducted using the same methodologies and procedures as a full special census, but it is for a subset of areas within the jurisdiction of the GU. The minimum statistical area for which any partial special census can be conducted is a 2020 Census tract.
An explanation of what is depicted on the BAS map, including what the various map symbols represent, should be provided. It is especially important to review the GUs boundaries at this meeting. An explanation of census tracts and boundaries is crucial, especially if the sponsor is conducting a partial Special Census.
In addition to updating the GU boundaries, including any annexations and/or detachments, the sponsor is also encouraged to add any street features and names missing from the BAS map during this review. This is especially important for areas of where there are newly built housing units and where the streets and their names may be missing from the census maps.
These updates made to the BAS maps are reflected on subsequent SC mapping products, including mapping products produced for data collection. Accurate field maps contribute to more efficient and accurate data collection.
The process for updating boundaries, the BAS forms, and the boundary certification process are included in the BAS how to guides. This guide is available online at: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/bas.html.
It is crucial that the GU reviews the maps carefully because the updates from this map are used to generate the governmental unit's Special Census Verification Map. Errors on the Special Census Verification map that require correction may delay the start of the SC.

title: Special Census Verification Map
content:
The Special Census Verification Map is produced from the information submitted by the sponsor on the Special Census Boundary and Annexation Survey Map. The Verification Map shows the Special Census Area (SCA) that will be included in the SC. The Special Census Verification Map shows updates the GU made to the BAS map.
It is crucial that the GU very carefully reviews the boundaries and all other updates that were submitted through the BAS to ensure the map properly reflects the SCA and the updates. All SC data collection products, i.e., the maps and address lists, are generated from a database benchmark based on the Special Census Verification Map.
Any errors on the Verification Map, once it has been certified as correct and returned to the Census Bureau, may result in an extended delay of the SC if anything must be changed or corrected.
Note: The Special Census Verification map is not an opportunity for the governmental unit to include additional areas in the SC. If the GU wishes to revise the SC area, additional costs and an extended timeline may be introduced into the SC process. Notify the RO Special Census manager immediately if the sponsor indicates there are errors or changes required to the Verification Map.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities Discussion
content:
During the initial contact with the GU, the RO (or designee) discusses the GUs responsibilities outlined in the Regional Director's letter. The GUs responsibilities include:
- Supplying office space.
- Supplying equipment, such as laptops and printers
- Recruiting.
- Planning for outreach.
- Planning for publicity.
Additional information about each of the governmental unit's responsibilities is provided below.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities: Supplying Office Space
content:
Ensure that the GU understands that they must provide the required office space to open a Special Census Office (SCO) and that whatever space is provided for the SCO must be compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the requirements of the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
If the space to house the SCO has been identified by the time of one of the initial meetings, the RO staff should inspect it, if possible.
SCO space requirements include:
- The office space should have a large open room for the field staff to meet with their supervisor and to receive supplies as necessary.
- Adequate parking should be available for the number of SCO staff and visiting field staff.
- The space must not be accessible by anyone other than the SC staff. It must contain enough locking file cabinets to secure confidential Title 13 and Personally Identifiable Information.
- An adequate number of tables and chairs must be provided, as outlined in the letter. Waste receptacles should also be provided.
- The GU is responsible for office maintenance, including trash removal. The sponsor must provide toilet paper and paper towels (if no hand dryer) for the restrooms.
Anyone providing maintenance services in the SCO must complete the Form BC-1759(SC), Special Sworn Status (SSS). This means, it is preferable that the same person (or persons) performs the maintenance services for the duration that the SCO is opened. See Topic 7 in Chapter 7 for more information about the Form BC-1759(SC), SSS.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities: Supplying Equipment
content:
Ensure that the GU understands the equipment requirements. The requirements for phone and Internet connections are important since installation of these telecommunications may require a significant lead team to install. Delay in the equipment installation can result in a delay of the SC.
The number of telephones required for the special census office depends on the size of the special census and the number of authorized office and field staff. Telephones must be non-cellular and connected to direct lines.
Because of the Census Bureau's privacy and confidentiality requirements, the lines cannot be routed through a switchboard or be part of the governmental unit's telephone network. If telephone lines must be installed, please check with the local telephone company regarding their installation timeline(s). Be aware that there can be a significant time from the request date until installation.
The Census Bureau attempts to minimize the amount of time and money a jurisdiction must spend to equip a special census office. Office furniture requirements are based on the need for simple work surfaces and the need to secure personally identifiable information protected under Title 13 of the U.S. Code.
At a minimum, each workstation should consist of a table and a chair. Desks are not necessary but can be provided for the special census supervisor and office clerks if they are available. Sufficient electrical outlets near each workstation are also required to support computers and a printer. Field staff will come into the special census office to meet with their supervisors and drop off work. Tables and chairs to use while reviewing materials are sufficient for these staff.
Locking vertical or lateral file cabinets are required to secure the Title 13 and personally identifiable information materials. Legal size cabinets are required to accommodate the oversized address registers and maps. The number of cabinets required is specified in the initial letter from the Census Bureau's regional director.
For this decade, the Census Bureau is requiring that GUs provide their own equipment and support. This allows for the GUs to use equipment they already possess as opposed to procuring it from the Census Bureau. This will decrease the overall cost to the GU. GUs should provide, at a minimum, computers (laptops or desktops), monitors if appropriate, printers, and barcode scanners. Detailed IT requirements will be provided to the GU through the Memorandum of Agreement process.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities: Recruiting
content:
In the initial visit with GU officials, recruiting needs should be discussed, including the number of applicants required and methods the governmental unit plans to use to attract applicants.
Generally, applicants are recruited at a rate of approximately three (3) to four (4) times the number of positions that are budgeted. The GU should recruit more applicants than the number of people who will be invited to training because experience has shown that (1) applicants may change their mind about working, (2) accept the job offer but do not show up for training, (3) complete the training but do not accept an assignment, or (4) drop their assignment before completing it. If there are any concerns by the GU or the Census Bureau that there may not be enough applicants for testing, this should be discussed, and a plan should be created to resolve the issue.
The discussion should include the GUs wishes regarding hiring from within the community. If not limited to those within the community, establish an acceptable distance (usually in miles) from a designated point for hiring staff. The GU should understand that field staff are paid time and mileage from their home to their assignments and any hiring of staff who live outside the acceptable distance may result in increased costs to the governmental for which they will be billed as indicated in the MOA.
The GU is also expected to provide ADA-compliant training space. In relatively small SCs, the SCO may suffice for this purpose. In larger SCs, where multiple, concurrent training sessions may be required, the GU may be asked to assist in securing additional space.
If there is a shortage of applicants in the local area and the local officials are unable to devise a plan to resolve the problem, contact the RO for guidance. The Census Bureau and perhaps the Special Census Supervisor specifically, may be asked to assist with recruiting.

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities: Planning for Outreach
content:
Outreach, education, and active promotion by the GU help to ensure a successful SC. Outreach:
- Helps in recruiting workers for the SC.
- Helps to educate residents about the importance of the SC to their community.
- Encourages residents to cooperate with Census workers.
The Special Census Program, Guidebook for Sponsors, provides a wealth of information on outreach. During the initial contact with the GU, the content of this handbook on outreach should be reviewed. In particular, the RO should suggest that the Special Census sponsor establish an Outreach Committee. This committee establishes partnerships within the GU and involves the residents.
This Outreach Committee is charged with developing announcements for SC jobs, publicizes the SC, especially in terms of benefits to the community, and encourages residents to cooperate with FRs when they visit households.
The Census Bureau provides several outreach materials to the GU. Most of the materials can be customized to the GUs needs. The GU is not required to use these materials and may wish to develop their own.
The data products are available from the Data Products tab on the Special Census Website at: <https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/specialcensus/data_products.html>
Materials include:
- Articles for Newsletters & Church Bulletins
- Articles & Announcements for local media outlets
- Talking points for meetings
- Flyers & Posters for distribution to local businesses
- Flyers & posters that can distributed by businesses to their patrons (for example, taped on pizza boxes)
- SC messages that can be placed on telephones, electronic bulletin boards, marquees, and websites
- SC messages that can be placed on utility/water bills
- Letter from the Highest Elected Official (HEO) about the SC

title: Governmental Unit Responsibilities: Planning for Publicity
content:
Publicity is important because it both generates applicants for census jobs and helps to motivate the community to respond to the SC.
The publicity effort should consist of articles and advertisements in the local newspaper(s) and other media outlets, including websites and social media. GUs are responsible for publicity with guidance from the RO.
The RO and GUs should arrange for publicity before the Special Census Date. The Special Census Date is the reference date for collecting the population and housing data.
The publicity should:
- Request cooperation from all residents of the community.
- Explain the value of the SC to the community.
Additional publicity, as required, should be planned during the SC.
GUs should have already run advertisements about the need for FRs, their pay rate, and the number of applicants needed, and how to apply. The GUs are responsible for all publicity-related costs.
For large SCs, the RO and the GU may consider enlisting local radio and TV stations to publicize the SC in public service announcements and in news coverage.
This page intentionally left blank.

title: Recruiting, Assessing, and Selecting Your Staff
content:
This chapter provides instructions for recruiting and selecting staff for the Special Census.
In a Special Census, is responsible for recruiting staff and ensuring that an adequate number of applicants are recruited. The Special Census Supervisor (or designee) is responsible for conducting applicant assessing.
Although recruiting is the responsibility of Special Census, the entire hiring process, including recruiting, application review, interviewing, and selecting, must comply with all federal employment rules and regulations. The Regional Office and Special Census Office are responsible for ensuring that Special Census employment processes follow all Census Bureau hiring procedures completely and are consistent with Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) principles. All qualified Special Census applicants will be considered without regard to non-merit factors such as race, gender, sexual orientation, national origin, color, religion, age, or disability. It is the responsibility of the Special Census Office (SCO) staff to monitor recruiting and adherence to EEO standards.

title: Recruiting Special Census Office and Field Staff
content:
## Recruiting Overview
The overall success of the Special Census ultimately depends on the field and office staff of the SCO. It is critical that the SCO management team understand the staffing requirements as outlined by the RO for each Special Census. The SCO management team is responsible for seeing that the pre- established staffing levels are met and maintained with qualified, temporary employees. The RO will provide the governmental unit in the initial letter the number of candidates to recruit for Special Census positions. A sample of this letter is included in Appendix E.

title: Recruiting Goals
content:
Recruiting is vital to the success of the Special Census. Successful recruiting will greatly increase the chances of a smooth and successful Special Census count.
It all starts with recruiting the right number of people, at the right time, in the right geographic areas. Pre-identified recruiting goals will be associated with each Special Census. These goals will be used to tell the governmental unit how many applicants must be recruited for that Special Census.

title: Recruiting the right number of people
content:
Recruiting the right number of people means meeting recruiting goals. Recruiting goals are aimed at getting the correct number of qualified applicants. A qualified applicant is one that meets the Census Bureau criteria for employment with the Special Census. It is important to keep in mind that all the people who go through application will not automatically become qualified applicants.
The recruiting goals are set based on many factors, including workload, anticipated staff turnover, expected numbers of unqualified applicants who will apply, and many other factors. Even though the goals may seem high, they are not!
A lot of historical information and experience has gone into setting those goals, and they are realistic. Check with the RO for more information about the recruiting plan and goals for the Special Census area.

title: Recruiting at the right time
content: Recruiting at the **right time** means meeting the recruiting goals by the stated deadlines. The Special Census consists of a series of carefully planned data collection activities that must be conducted on schedule. We must have a large enough pool of applicants before selection and hiring begins. This ensures hiring can be completed on time to begin and complete the Special Census on schedule.

title: Recruiting from the right geographic area
content:
Recruiting from the right geographic areas means making sure we have recruited from the right communities and neighborhoods. We want our workforce to be representative of the Special Census area. Having a diverse applicant pool representative of all the neighborhoods within the Special Census Area is important for many reasons.
The work that we hire people to do is done in all neighborhoods included in the Special Census Area. This work involves getting people in each Special Census Area neighborhood to cooperate and to answer questions about their address and household.
When we recruit and hire people from a neighborhood to work in that neighborhood, we have more success in gaining cooperation from the public. People are more willing to respond to someone they recognize as a neighbor or fellow member of the community.
Additionally, hiring people who live in the neighborhoods that they will work in saves money because field staff are paid time and mileage from the time they leave their homes to go out to work until the time they return home. Efficient work assignments with minimal travel required results in lower operational costs.

title: Recruiting Job Applicants
content: One of the Special Census Supervisor's first responsibility when assigned to a Special Census will be to talk with the governmental unit about its recruiting strategy and to monitor the governmental unit's success at its recruiting activities. As needed, the Special Census Supervisor and the RO will assist in the recruiting efforts to secure the required number of job applicants. The governmental unit, however, should be made to understand that if the Special Census Supervisor must become involved with assisting in recruiting enough job applicants, this may increase the cost of the Special Census for the governmental unit.

title: Recruitment Publicity Strategies
content:
The governmental unit handbook that is provided by the Census Bureau to each governmental unit contains many suggestions of recruiting strategies that have proven effective for the Census Bureau.
Getting the word out for Special Census job opportunities in various locations is important. Sometimes people need to get the message that the Census Bureau is recruiting applicants for the Special Census Area from more than one source before they call to apply.
Distributing the recruiting message in more than one type of medium is also important. It may be useful to place advertisements in the local newspaper, have local radio stations make public service announcements, or post a notice on the local government's sponsor website about the need for Special Census workers.
In addition, the SCO and the governmental unit can publicize the need for applicants using two possible strategies:
- One strategy is to approach the general population. For example, the governmental unit might pay and place an ad in the local newspaper announcing the Special Census job opportunities to get the message about Special Census jobs out to as many people as possible.
- The other strategy is to target specific groups. This might include the unemployed, retirees, people who work part- time or full-time, contingent workforce (including those who are self-employed or who change jobs frequently, moving in and out of the workforce), people who work at home, and volunteers.
Applicants interested in applying for Special Census positions will be directed to the online application web site. There will be no paper applications accepted for Special Census unless a reasonable accommodation is required. The RO will monitor the application process and work with the SCO so that recruitment goals are met.
If enough applicants are not available, the Special Census staff must expedite the recruiting process immediately. The governmental unit must be informed that additional recruiting efforts are needed and may result in additional costs. The Special Census Supervisor should consult regularly with the governmental unit regarding their recruiting efforts to date.

title: Potential Applicant Sources
content:
As needed, the following places may be useful as recruiting sources:
- State employment office.
- Student employment office at any local college or university.
- Fraternal and veteran organizations.
- Local chamber of commerce.
- Community-based organizations such as the Urban League, NAACP, Sons of Italy, B'nai B'rith, and so on.
- Churches.
- Interested people identified by other SC employees or managers.

title: Monitoring the GU's Progress in Meeting Recruiting Goals
content:
Because the Census Bureau does not have direct responsibility for recruiting applicants, there may be some unique challenges to ensuring that the three recruiting goals: (1) the right number, (2) at the right time, and (3) in the right neighborhoods are met.
It is the responsibility of the Special Census Supervisor to closely monitor the governmental unit's progress in meeting the pre-identified recruiting goals and to provide suggestions and assistance as needed. Some of the governmental unit's recruiting strategies that should monitored include:
- Making sure the governmental unit understands the volume of applicants needed.
- Making sure the governmental unit is getting enough people interested in applying for short-term, temporary jobs. This can only be accomplished through repeated, widespread exposure to compelling messages about census jobs.
- Helping the governmental unit determine where and when to place recruiting message. Placing these messages is key and the governmental unit handbook provides a wealth of suggestions on how to do this successfully.

title: Special Census Personnel
content:
## Overview
The staff for a Special Census may include a Supervisor, Field Managers (FM), Field Supervisors (FS), Field Representatives (FRs), clerks. Except for the Special Census Supervisor, all staff positions for a Special Census are generally recruited and hired locally.
Staffing levels for a Special Census are based on several factors including the size and estimated workload of the Special Census area. Headquarters (HQ) issues guidelines for staffing which includes the number of persons needed for each position and the number of hours and days budgeted for the position. All the positions listed above may not be necessary. Additionally, the time frame needed to conduct the Special Census may both affect and change staffing needs accordingly. For example, for a Special Census with an estimated population greater than 50,000, the SCO may be authorized additional positions.

title: Field Representatives
content:
FRs are responsible for the following types of activities:
- Assembling and packing the Census Bureau carrying bag with the materials needed for the day, such as the Lenel Badge, SC-1202, Special Census Field Representative Manual, SC-1(F), Information Sheet, etc.
- Locating and traveling to their Assignment Area (AA).
- Canvassing each block in their AAs to identify places where people can live.
- Conducting an interview at each structure to determine if it contains housing units.
- Verifying the Special Census Date status of each housing unit in their AA.
- Updating the SC-920*,* Address Listing Page, in the Address Register.
- Conducting an interview at each designated address using the SC-1, Field Representative Questionnaire.
- Completing a BC-27, Time, Attendance, and Cost Report and a BC-27A, Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses for each day census work is performed.
FRs may also receive additional training to conduct the enumeration at Group Quarters (GQ) and Transitory Locations (TL), if these types of places exist in the Special Census area.
Refer to Chapters 14 and 15 for more information about GQs and TLs. The Field Representatives responsibilities are described in detail in the SC-1202, Special Census Field Representative Manual.

title: Field Supervisors
content:
FSs lead and direct a team of FRs. Generally, if a Special Census requires fewer than 10 FRs, the Special Census Supervisor may assume the duties of the Field Supervisor. However, regardless of the number of FRs, there will always be at least one FS.
The FSs are responsible for:
- Inventorying Special Census FR assignment packages and other forms and materials to ensure they have an ample supply.
- Becoming familiar with their Field Supervisor Area (FSA). Looking for areas with potential enumeration challenges, such as high growth areas or anything else that may impact the Special Census enumeration.
- Training FRs if instructed to do so by the Special Census Field Manager.
- Distributing assignments to each FR on their team.
- Conducting an initial observation with each FR on their team.
- Meeting daily with FRs to:
- Review completed SC-1s, Field Representative Questionnaires, Address Registers, and maps.
- May review the BC-27, Time, Attendance, and Cost Report and a BC-27A, Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses for completeness and accuracy.
- Answer questions and provide feedback.
- Update the SC-20, Field Supervisor's Management Record by entering the housing unit count, person count, and hours and miles for each Field Representative on the team.
- Meeting with the supervisor daily to turn in completed work and to report progress of the Special Census.
- Providing on-the-job training (OJT) and other assistance to the FRs, if time permits.
- Conducting quality assurance activities:
- Dependent Quality Check (DQC).
- Repair address registers and maps, as needed.
- Reinterview.
- Recanvass Assignment Areas (AAs) that do not contain any housing units.
- Visiting and enumerating households that refuse to cooperate with the FRs.
- Reassigning or assisting with AAs that FRs were unable to complete because of difficult or unusual circumstances.
- Monitoring FRs performance to ensure the Special Census is completed on time and within budget.
- Providing procedures for safety, accidents, and injuries (if required).
The FSs responsibilities are described in detail in the SC-1130, Special Census Field Supervisor's Manual.

title: Clerks
content:
Clerks may perform a variety of office operations including:
- Assembling training materials.
- Preparing questionnaires and address registers for assignment.
- Preparing work assignments for Field Representatives, Field Supervisors, and Field operations supervisors.
- Checking work out to the field in MOJO.
- Reviewing incoming address registers, questionnaires, and payroll forms for completeness, consistency, and legibility.
- Performing a QA review of address registers and/or SC-1, *Field Representative Questionnaires,* and identifying cases that require a field check.
- Keying BC-27 and BC-27A data into the GovTA system.
- Shipping materials to the RO and/or the National Processing Center.

title: Special Census Office and Field Staff Candidates
content:
## Overview
FR job applicants for Field Representative position must apply online through USA Jobs before they can be considered for employment. Applicants for the position of Field Supervisor or Clerk, if authorized for the Special Census, must meet the qualification requirements posted on the Job vacancy announcement.
The Special Census Supervisor and his or her staff must:
- Ensure online sites are identified.
- Ensure an adequate number of applicants are aware of the vacancy.
- Ensure all EEO principals are followed and that applicants with disabilities receive proper and equal consideration.

title: Hiring Waivers
content: The Special Census Program does not have a waiver to hire federal retirees, including postal retirees, without offsetting their annuity. The only exception is for military retirees, who are eligible to be hired.

title: Federal Employment Requirements and Policies
content:
## Citizenship
Only United States Citizens will be considered for census jobs.

title: Age
content: To be eligible to work for the Census Bureau, applicants must be at least 18 years old at the time they enter on duty.

title: Nepotism
content:
Nepotism (*favoritism shown based on family relationships*) is prohibited. The Census Bureau will monitor restrictions on the employment of relatives to ensure that Census officials do not advocate one of their relatives for employment, promotion, or advancement. In addition, no relative of an employee may be employed or assigned to any position in which the employee may be able to directly or indirectly supervise, control, or influence the work or employment status of the relative or the affairs of the organizational unit to which the relative is to be assigned. This includes promotions from a FR to FS that would result in any supervision of a relative.
A relative is defined as: father, mother, son, daughter, brother, sister, uncle, aunt, first cousin, nephew, niece, husband, wife, father-in law, mother-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, stepfather, stepmother, stepson, stepdaughter, stepbrother, stepsister, half-brother, or half-sister.
Nepotism is reviewed by the NPC HR Speciallists during the onboarding process.

title: Dual Federal Employment
content:
The Dual Compensation Act (PL-88-448) prohibits federal employees from working more than 40 regular hours per week for more than one federal agency; therefore, you **may not** hire an applicant who already has a full-time federal job under any circumstances. Although the law allows more than one part-time federal position, you must refer all dual employment applications to the RO for approval before an offer of employment can be made.
Issues with Dual Federal Employment for field staff will be handled by your NPC HR Specialist.

title: Retired Federal Annuitants
content:
If the applicate is a Retired Federal Annuitants, the salary would need to be offset to determine eligibility.
Retired Federal Annuitants for field staff will be handled by your NPC HR Specialist.

title: Retired Railroad Employees
content: Current or retired railroad workers are not federal employees. Thus, they are not affected by the *Dual Compensation Act* and should be treated as any other applicant for a Census Bureau position.

title: Former/Current Tax Collectors or Law Enforcement Workers
content:
All incompatible employment must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis for compatibility with Census Bureau employment. This policy in no way implies a negative assessment of these occupations, or the trustworthiness of applicants; rather it reflects our sensitivity toward public perception and the critical need for public cooperation. Some examples of incompatible employment could include law enforcement, tax collection, immigration, etc.
Incompatible employment situations will be handled by your NPC HR Specialist.

title: Military Annuitants
content: Under the provisions of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2000 (P.L. 106-65), reductions in retired or retainer pay are no longer required for retired members of a uniformed service who are employed in a civilian office or position of the U.S. Government.

title: Debarment of Applicants Not Registered with the Selective Service System
content:
An applicant's Selective Service registration can be verified on the Internet at [https://www.sss.gov/verify/.](https://www.sss.gov/verify/)
If a male applicant is between 18 and 25 and is required to register, but has not done so, he is eligible for appointment **only after** registering. If he states that he is not registered but has proof of military service as a veteran, or part-time National Guard or Reservist he is eligible for appointment. If the applicant is required to register, but refuses to do so, or has not registered as of his 26^th^ birthday, inform him that a decision on his eligibility will have to be made by the Regional Director. If male applicants who otherwise meet the criteria for registration are not registered, **do not hire** them unless a favorable determination is made by your NPC HR Specialist..
These situations will be resolved by your NPC HR Specialist.

title: Restrictions on the Political Activities of Employees
content:
Under the 1939 Hatch Act, federal employees, among others, faced significant restrictions on their ability to participate in political activities. Congress amended the Hatch Act in 1993 to permit political activity by federal employees.
With the 1993 amendments, many federal employees now are permitted to take an active part in political management or in political campaigns. The Department of Commerce (DOC), of which the Census Bureau is part, is covered by the 1993 amendments; thereby, enabling Bureau employees to participate more freely in political activities.
The following Do's and Don'ts provide a summary of political activities:

title: Federal Hatch Act Do's
content:
Census employees covered by the 1993 amendments **may**:
- Be candidates for public office in nonpartisan (not affiliated with political parties) elections. However, if elected, employees must resign Census Bureau appointment or decline the elected position.
- Register and vote as they choose.
- Assist in voter registration drives.
- Express opinions about candidates and issues.
- Contribute money to political organizations, candidate, or party.
- Attend political fund-raising functions.
- Attend and be active at political rallies and meetings.
- Join and be an active member of a political party or club.
- Sign nominating petitions.
- Campaign for or against referendum questions, constitutional amendments, municipal ordinances.
- Campaign for or against candidates in partisan elections.
- Make campaign speeches for candidates in partisan elections.
- Distribute campaign literature in partisan elections.
- Hold office in political clubs or parties.

title: Federal Hatch Act Don'ts
content:
Census employees covered by 1993 amendments **may not:**
- Use official authority or influence to interfere with an election.
- Solicit or discourage political activity of anyone with business before their agency.
- Solicit or receive political contributions. (You may solicit or accept political contributions if you are a member of a union, and the solicitation are to another member of the union who is not a subordinate employee.)
- Be candidates for public office in partisan elections.
- Wear political buttons on duty.
- Solicit or accept volunteer services from a subordinate.
- Engage in political activity while:
- on duty.
- in a government office.
- wearing an official uniform.
- using a government vehicle.

title: Federal Hatch Act Summary
content: The *Do's and Don'ts* listed above are intended to provide an overview of permissible activities and restrictions; the listing is not intended as comprehensive reference of the Department of Commerce; hence, Census Bureau's, policies relating to employee participation in political activities. While the primary responsibility in the Federal Government for provision of advisory opinion and enforcement functions relating to the Hatch Act rests with the U. S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC), your first contact for questions should be with the Census Bureau's Employee Relations Branch, phone 301-763-3701.

title: Other Conditions of Employment
content:
In addition, eligibility requirements, all applicants must meet the following criteria:
- Field staff (such as, Field Representative, Field Supervisor) must reside in the area where a major part of the work assignment is located.
- Have a valid driver's license.
- Be able to hear responses and to read questionnaires, given reasonable accommodation.
- Be able to attend occasional training sessions away from home.
- Be able to work several hours per day which often includes a lot of walking and climbing stairs.
- Be available for day, evening, and weekend work, as needed.

title: Selective Factors
content:
Selective factors are skills, abilities, or knowledge that are essential for the performance of the duties and responsibilities of the position. The selective factor must be listed on the recruitment bulletin to be used when making a selection. Applicants who do not meet a selective factor are ineligible for further consideration for that opening.
For field positions, the only applicable selective factor is language.

title: Employment Suitability Issues
content:
Do not delay your preparation of a Selection Certificate if doing so will interfere with the timely completion of Special Census work. You may issue the certificate pending suitability review of CIS. *However, you must hold a position available for any preference eligible pending suitability review*.
Suitability issues involve the applicant or employee's character, reputation, trustworthiness, and fitness as related to the efficiency of the federal service. General factors that must be considered are: (1) whether the conduct of the individual may reasonably be expected to interfere or prevent effective performance in the position applied for or employed in, and (2) whether the conduct of the individual may reasonably be expected to interfere with or prevent effective performance of the duties and responsibilities of the SCO.
Suitability issues with be determined by Census Investigative Services and/or the Employee Relations Branch. ERB will notify the RO of any issues.

title: Outside Employment Issues
content:
The Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) prohibits outside activities that are incompatible with fulfilling a federal employee's duties and responsibilities. Two major considerations are:
- Outside activities must not involve, or appear to involve, a conflict of interest.
- Outside activities must not interfere with or be detrimental to the efficient completion of official duties during the hours an employee is expected to be available for census work. An employee's involvement in outside activities must not in any way affect the public trust or effective performance of official business.
Generally, the Census Bureau does not hire individuals currently employed in the law or regulatory enforcement professions (for example, police officers, tax collectors, or tax assessors) or other applicants whose primary employment may be perceived by the public as potentially being incompatible with the Census Bureau's legal mandate to maintain the confidentiality of census data.
However, all non-Census employment, including law and regulatory enforcement jobs will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis for compatibility with Census Bureau employment policy.
This policy in no way implies a negative assessment of these occupations, or the trustworthiness of such applicants; rather, it reflects our sensitivity toward public perception and the critical need for public cooperation.
Employees are not required to seek agency approval for outside employment or activities. However, employees are responsible for ensuring that their outside employment and other outside activities comply with the provisions set forth in the *Standards of Ethical Conduct for Employees of the Executive Branch (title 5, Code of Federal Regulation, Part 2635), Subpart H- Outside Activities*.
Employees who wish to engage in outside employment or other outside activities must comply with all relevant statutes, regulations, and provisions including, when applicable:
- The prohibition on outside employment, or other outside activity that conflicts with the employee's official duties.
- The restriction that employees shall not serve, other than on behalf of the United States as an expert witness with or without compensation, in any proceeding before a court or agency of the United States in which the United States is a party or has a direct and substantial interest, unless the employee's participation is authorized by the agency.
- The limitations on receipt of outside earned income by certain Presidential appointees and other non-career employees.
- The limitations on participation in professional organizations.
- The limitations on paid and unpaid teaching, speaking, and writing.
- The limitations on fund-raising activities.
Advise all employees to consult with their supervisor on any outside employment or other activity to ensure that their participation in such activity does not raise a question of conflict of interest, or conflicts with the Standards of Ethical Conduct for Employees of the Executive Service.

title: Selecting Job Applicants
content: All selections will be made in USA Staffing. Refer to ROAM 2024-07 for guidance on selecting and hiring Special Census staff.

title: Training and Appointing Your Staff
content: Applicants selected for employment need to attend two different sessions scheduled by the Special Census Office (SCO). Selected trainees will first attend a one-day session to be photographed and badged. Those trainees that pass the background check will be invited to attend an operational training, also referred as job-specific training. This chapter provides instructions for training staff for the Special Census.

title: Admin Training and Operational Training
content:
Training is divided into two types of training---Admin training and operational, or job-specific, training.
Field staff selected for employment will be invited first to Admin training. Admin training is where trainees will complete badging operations. Field Supervisors (FS) and Field Representative (FR) staff will receive Lenel Badges, and Office Staff will receive Homeland Security Presidential Directive (HSPD-12) Badges.
Operational training is the job specific training the trainee will receive to conduct the enumeration during the Special Census. They will also:
- Be trained on how to complete payroll forms.
- Be trained on personal safety.
- Complete the No Fear Act training.
The Special Census Supervisor or Field Manager trains the Field Supervisor, first presenting the Field Supervisor with the Field Representative training then the Field Supervisor training.
The Field Supervisor in turn trains the Field Representatives in their crew.

title: Preparing for Training Sessions
content:
## Find and Inspect a Training Site
The RO will provide guidance for securing training space. Training space requirements depend on the size of the workload for the Special Census area. For example, training might be given at the SCO if the space can accommodate the number of trainees invited for training. In some situations, the RO might have already arranged with the governmental unit to use local government space.
In other situations, the Special Census Supervisor might need to locate training space if no previous arrangements were made. The Special Census Supervisor can ask the governmental unit for assistance in locating training space or refer to *Suggestions for Potential Training Sites*.
The training space **must be rent-free.** If a rent-free facility requires a signed agreement, contact the RO immediately. The Special Census Supervisor does not have the authority to sign any agreements to rent space. Many facilities use agreements that may contain an indemnity clause, and no one, not even a Regional Director, is authorized to indemnify the federal government.
In some cases, especially when a cascaded training approach is utilized, Field Supervisors may need to locate their own training space. Field Supervisors will be trained to locate training space if needed.
The Special Census Supervisor needs to remind Field Supervisors to not sign any agreements with facilities, even if the facility is rent free.

title: Requirements That a Training Site Must Meet
content:
The training site must:
- Be rent-free. If free space is not available, do not make a commitment to rent the training site.
- Be available for the days when training is scheduled.
- Be quiet and free of distractions.
- Be large enough to accommodate all the trainees.
- Be handicapped accessible.
- Have sufficient desks or table space.
- Be heated, cooled, or well ventilated, as weather requires.
- Have available restrooms.
- Have adequate parking if trainees are driving to the session.
- Have eating facilities nearby. If unable to locate a site that meets this requirement, the SCO needs to ensure to tell the trainees to bring their lunches when they are notified about the training session.
- Be as centrally located as possible in the SCOs for group training. This minimizes travel time by all trainees.

title: Suggestions for Potential Training Sites
content:
Use the following suggestions as potential sites:
- City halls or municipal buildings
- City, county, or federal courthouses
- Post offices
- Military reserve centers, National Guard armories, or military bases
- Other government offices if these are not law enforcement agencies
- Veteran's organization halls
- Club or lodge meeting halls
- Churches, synagogues, or mosques
- Community or recreation centers
- Firehouses
- Libraries
- Schools, including colleges or technical institutes
If the SCO schedules more than one training course session for Field Representatives, the clerks will create a Field Representative training session for each scheduled session. The clerks, while creating the operational training session, will also create the Admin Day training session for that specific training session.
The facility and course session information will be provided to the clerks.

title: Inviting Applicants to Admin Day Training
content:
Do not invite anyone that has not completed their onboarding documents in USA Staffing and have cleared.
Applicants will be selected for employment following the guidelines indicated in *Selecting Job Applicants* -- Applicants are invited to their training when they have:
- Been selected.
- Completed their onboarding documents.
- Cleared their background investigation.

title: Badging Personnel
content:
With the introduction of the new USA Staffing hiring procedures, the badging process is quick. Once the new hire completes various paperwork, the Regional Office (RO) will prepare the badges.
The RO Administrative department delivers the Field Supervisor and Field Representative LENEL badges, along with a letter to be signed by employee, to the Special Census Office. After collecting the signed letters, the SCO returns them to the RO and the badging is complete.

title: Training Field Staff
content:
Trainees that pass the background check will be invited to a job- specific (operational) training. The type of training conducted, either group or cascaded training, will usually determines who notifies the trainees of the place, date, and time to attend the job-specific training.
The trainer will verify and confirm that the training space is available for the scheduled training days. The trainer will also take and record attendance on the for each day of training. At the end of training, the trainer will forward the completed list to the SCO.

title: Training Packages
content:
Both Field Supervisors and Field Representative trainees receive a training package as part of their classroom training. Additionally, Field Supervisors and Field Representatives receive a production supply package containing extra materials needed for their respective jobs.
Depending on RO guidance, training and supply packages may be preassembled and shipped to the SCO or the materials are sent to the SCO for clerks to assemble the kits. If the Field Representative and Field Supervisor training and supply packages are not prepackaged and shipped to the SCO, the SCO will receive the training and supply contents in bulk. In this case, the RO will provide necessary instructions to assemble the kits. The SC-50.1, *SCO Job Aids* contains the instructions and checklists on how to assemble the training and supply packages. These must be assembled prior to training. The training and supply package contents are also included in each of the field staff training guides.

title: Training
content: The Special Census Supervisor or Field Manager is responsible for training Field Supervisors and clerks, if authorized. If Field Supervisors are not authorized, the Special Census Supervisor will train the Field Representatives.

title: Training Field Supervisors
content:
Train Field Supervisors in a classroom training session using Form SC-1230, *Guide for Training Field Supervisors*. The FS trainees learn about their job as a supervisor as well as gain a better understanding of the job of a Field Representative. 
If there is only one Field Supervisor authorized for a small Special Census, train the Field Supervisor along with the Field Representatives during the Field Representative training session. Then, immediately conduct the Field Supervisor training session the day following the Field Representative training session.

title: Training Field Representatives
content:
In a larger Special Census, Field Supervisors train their own Field Representatives. Form SC-1204, *Guide for Training Field Representatives*, is used to conduct the classroom training for Field Representatives.
The Special Census Supervisor needs to contact the RO if additional Field Representatives need to be trained due to termination or resignations. The RO may authorize the Special Census Supervisor to conduct replacement training.

title: Training Office Clerks
content:
It is expected that clerks also attend the Field Representative training. Clerks should be on board by the time Field Representative training is scheduled for Field Representatives.
Clerks need to attend Field Representative training so they can learn the Special Census listing and enumeration procedures. Clerks may need to complete SC-Q, Special Census Questionnaire by telephone if a respondent calls the SCO.
The clerks also need to learn and understand the Special Census enumeration procedures to conduct the office quality assurance activities in the office. Clerks compare questionnaires completed by Field Representatives against the reinterview questionnaire to determine if the Field Representative followed Special Census enumeration procedures.
