title: Equal Employment Opportunity Program
content: This chapter contains the Census Bureau's Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) policies and the responsibilities of the Special Census Office (SCO) concerning the Census Bureau's EEO programs.

title: EEO Introduction and Definitions
content:
## EEO Introduction and Definitions
EEO is the right of all persons to be able to apply and be evaluated for job opportunities without regard to such non-merit factors as race, sex, (including pregnancy, gender identity, and sexual orientation) national origin, color, religion, age, reprisal, genetic information, or disability. The Census Bureau will not tolerate any form of unlawful discrimination, including sexual harassment. All applicants and employees have a right to freedom from retaliation for filing an EEO complaint, participating in the EEO complaint process, or opposing unlawful discrimination.

title: Federal Laws
content:
The following federal laws govern the EEO program throughout the federal government.
In addition, regulations of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) forbid restraint, interference, coercion, discrimination, or reprisal at any stage in the processing of an employment complaint under the laws above, including the counseling stage.
- *Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964*, as amended. This act protects all employees and applicants from employment discrimination based on race, color, gender, religion, sexual orientation, and national origin.
- *Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) of 1967*, as amended. This act protects employees and applicants who are 40 years or older from employment discrimination based on age.
- *Rehabilitation Act of 1973*. This act protects qualified individuals with disabilities from employment discrimination based on disability.
- *Equal Pay Act of 1963*. This act protects employees from discrimination based on sex in pay for equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibilities.
- *The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (GINA).* Under Title II of GINA, it is illegal to discriminate against employees or applicants because of genetic information. Title II of GINA prohibits the use of genetic information (i.e., family medical history) in making employment decisions, restricts employers from requesting, requiring, or purchasing genetic information, and strictly limits the disclosure of genetic information.
- *The Pregnancy Discrimination Act*. This law amended Title VII to make it illegal to discriminate against a woman because of pregnancy, childbirth, or a medical condition related to pregnancy or childbirth. The law also makes it illegal to retaliate against a person because the person complained about discrimination, filed a charge of discrimination, or participated in an employment discrimination investigation or lawsuit.
- Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA).
- Section 102 and 103 of the Civil Rights Act of 1991.
All employees should be made aware of the Census Bureau's EEO policy at the time of training. Applicants should be advised by display of EEO posters in the SCO and at recruiting/testing sites.

title: EEO Policy Statement
content:
The Census Bureau is committed to equal opportunity for all persons without regard to race, sex, sexual orientation and gender identity, pregnancy, sexual harassment, national origin, color, religion, age, GINA, equal compensation, retaliation, or disability.
Managers, supervisors, and employees alike have responsibilities to ensure that the Census Bureau's actions foster an environment of equal opportunity in the workplace. Policies, practices, procedures, and actions must be free of unlawful discrimination. This includes all aspects of personnel management and their effects upon the hiring, placement, training, advancement, and retention of qualified individuals. Sexual harassment is prohibited, and steps will be taken to eliminate it when it exists. Employees have the right to seek redress from alleged discrimination and will be protected from reprisal in exercising this right.

title: EEO Staff and Other Stakeholders
content:
## EEO Program
The EEO Officer and staff oversee the Census Bureau's EEO Program. The Office of Equal Opportunity and Diversity & Inclusion is located, 4600 Silver Hill Road, Washington, DC 20233. The telephone numbers include toll-free (800) 872-6096, select 1; (301) 763-2853, select 1; or by email at eeo.general.mailbox@census.gov. The EEO staff includes EEO Specialists/Counselors engaged in the processing of complaints of employment discrimination through telephone counseling services from Census Headquarters (HQ).

title: EEO Officer
content:
The EEO officer performs the following duties:
- Administers the Census Bureau's discrimination resolution system.
- Ensures a continuing program of education and training for supervisors and managers.
- Designs a campaign to publicize the Census Bureau's EEO Program to all employees to provide notice of time limits and necessity of contacting a counselor before filing a complaint and the telephone numbers and address of the EEO Office.
- Provides guidance to all EEO Specialists and Counselors.
- Advises Regional Directors (RDs) of the responsibilities and objectives of EEO Specialists/Counselors and the importance of cooperating with the Counselors as they attempt informal resolution of EEO complaints by employees and applicants for employment.
- Directs the development of multi-year and annual affirmative employment program plans and annual accomplishment reports.

title: EEO Specialists/Counselors
content:
The EEO Officer appoints all EEO Specialists/Counselors. Anyone who wishes to seek informal counseling through the EEO complaint process **must** contact the EEO Office at Census Headquarters. No EEO Counselors are located at the SCO.
The EEO Counselor has six clearly defined duties that must be performed for each completed counseling session:
- Advises the aggrieved about the EEO complaint process, under 29 CFR 1614 rights and responsibilities, and other election requirements.
- Determines the issue(s) and basis(es) of the alleged complaint.
- Conducts a limited inquiry for the purposes of furnishing information for settlement efforts and determining jurisdictional questions if a formal complaint is filed.
- Seeks a resolution of the matter at the lowest possible level.
- Documents the resolution or advises the aggrieved of their right to file a formal discrimination complaint if resolution fails.
- Prepares a report sufficient to determine that required counseling actions have been taken and resolves any jurisdictional questions that may arise.

title: Manager/Supervisor EEO Responsibilities
content:
## Chief, Field Division
The Chief, Field Division (FLD), as overseer for each SCO:
- Reviews EEO accomplishments.
- Establishes and monitors affirmative employment objectives.
- Holds Regional Directors accountable for meeting their EEO responsibilities by evaluating them on their efforts.
- Takes prompt and effective corrective action where appropriate.

title: Regional Directors
content:
Each Regional Director achieves successful EEO when they:
- Provide opportunities for all employees to have assignments that are consistent with their capabilities.
- Ensure that EEO Program posters (Employment Discrimination is against the law!) are displayed in prominent places throughout the workspace.
- Use available training and work experience which give employees opportunities for personal growth.
- Implement affirmative employment policy and program objectives.
- Enforce accountability by subordinate supervisors.
- Ensure that personnel selection practices consider reasonable accommodation (RA).
- Communicate to the Chief, FLD, Human Resource Division (HRD), Administrative and Customer Services Division, and the EEO Office on EEO matters that should be considered in the formulation of policies and programs.

title: Line Supervisors
content:
All Line Supervisors, in a position of authority directly over an employee, must:
- Apply the EEO policies and objectives in accomplishing the work of the Census Bureau.
- Apply EEO principles in every aspect of the work.
- Ensure EEO Program posters are displayed in prominent places throughout the workspace.
- Counsel subordinates.
- Consider structuring the work in a manner that would allow for increased career opportunities for lesser-skilled employees.
- Maintain an atmosphere free of unlawful discrimination by:
- Demonstrating awareness of EEO laws and policies; for example, preventing sexual harassment and providing reasonable accommodation for individuals with disabilities.
- Taking appropriate action against employees who violate EEO principles; that is, counsel, discipline, and remove when necessary.
- Cooperating with EEO Specialists, Counselors, and Investigators.
- Seeking resolution to allegations and complaints of discrimination.

title: EEO Offenses and Guidelines
content:
## Unlawful Discrimination Offense
Unlawful Discrimination is a specific act(s) that denies employees tangible employment benefits because of their Race, Color, National Origin, Sex (includes Gender Identity, Sexual Preference, or Gender Stereotype and Sexual Harassment), Religion, Age, Genetic Information, or Disability.
Retaliation is the most frequently alleged basis of discrimination in the federal sector and the most common discrimination finding in federal sector cases.
EEO laws prohibit punishing job applicants or employees for asserting their rights to be free from employment discrimination including harassment. Asserting these EEO rights is called protected activity, and it can take many forms. For example, it is unlawful to retaliate against applicants or employees for:
- Filing or being a witness in an EEO charge, complaint, investigation, or lawsuit.
- Communicating with a supervisor or manager about employment discrimination, including harassment.
- Answering questions during an employer investigation of alleged harassment.
- Refusing to follow orders that would result in discrimination.
- Resisting sexual advances or intervening to protect others.
- Requesting accommodation of a disability or for a religious practice.
- Asking managers or co-workers about salary information to uncover potentially discriminatory wages.
Participating in a complaint process is protected from retaliation under all circumstances. Other acts to oppose discrimination are protected if the employee was acting on a reasonable belief that something in the workplace may violate EEO laws, even if he or she did not use legal terminology to describe it.
Engaging in EEO activity, however, does not shield an employee from all discipline or discharge. Employers are free to discipline or terminate workers if motivated by *non-retaliatory and non-discriminatory* reasons that would otherwise result in such consequences. However, an employer is not allowed to do anything in response to EEO activity that would discourage someone from resisting or complaining about future discrimination.
For example, depending on the facts, it could be retaliation if an employer acts because of the employee\'s EEO activity to:
- Reprimand the employee or give a performance evaluation that is lower than it should be.
- Transfer the employee to a less desirable position.
- Engage in verbal or physical abuse.
- Make or threaten to make reports to authorities (such as reporting immigration status or contacting the police).
- Increase scrutiny.
- Spread false rumors, treat a family member negatively (for example, cancel a contract with the person\'s spouse).
- Make the person\'s work more difficult (for example, punishing an employee for an EEO complaint by purposefully changing his work schedule to conflict with family responsibilities).

title: What is Sexual Harassment
content:
The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) guidelines state that harassment based on sex is a violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended. Unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, and other verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature is sexual harassment when:
- Submission to such conduct is made either explicitly or implicitly a term or condition of an individual\'s employment.
- Submission to or rejection of such conduct by an individual is used as the basis for employment decisions affecting such individual.
- Such conduct has the purpose or effect of:
- Unreasonably interfering with an individual\'s work performance.
- Creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment.
There are two forms of sexual harassment, Quid-Pro-Quo and Sexual Harassment, Hostile work environment. Quid-Pro-Quo (this for that) occurs when the person engaging in the harassment can control a tangible employment benefit over the person being harassed. Tangible employment benefits include, but not limited to, promotions, demotions, training, assignments, etc. Hostile work environment occurs when the conduct is so severe and pervasive that it interferes with an employee's work performance or creates and intimidating, hostile or offensive work environment.

title: Census Bureau Policy Statement
content:
It is the U.S. Census Bureau's policy that all employees must be allowed to work in an environment free from sexual harassment. Sexual harassment is a form of sex discrimination prohibited under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended. Sexual harassment is unacceptable conduct in the workplace and will not be tolerated. Employees engaging in sexual harassment or unlawful discrimination will be subject to disciplinary action, up to and including removal.
It is important that all employees understand the law and the policy and take all steps within their power to ensure that this form of discrimination does not exist within the Census Bureau.
Thus, recognizing that there are many forms of sexual harassment, the Census Bureau, in accordance with case law, will not tolerate nor condone the following:
- Unwelcome verbal suggestive remarks, sexual insults, innuendoes, jokes, and humor about sex or gender-specific traits, sexual propositions, and threats.
- Unwelcome nonverbal suggestive or insulting sounds, leering/ogling, whistling, gestures of a sexual nature, and sexually graphic materials.
- Unwanted physical contact, including but not limited to, cornering, touching, pinching, brushing the body, and actual or attempted rape or assault.
Neither the Census Bureau's e-mail system nor computer equipment should be used to transmit or download material of a sexually graphic nature. The Census Bureau policy on sexual harassment applies to all employees and covers harassment between supervisors and subordinates, between employees, by employees outside the workplace while conducting government business, and by nonemployees while conducting business in the Census Bureau's workplace.

title: Responsibilities in the Charge Against Sexual Harassment
content:
Each employee should play a role in the prevention or elimination of sexual harassment by:
- Examining their behavior on the job.
- Supporting the Census Bureau's policy against sexual harassment.
- Identifying and taking individual action to stop inappropriate behavior by communicating directly and immediately with the person(s) whose behavior is offensive.
- Notifying their supervisor, higher level manager, EEO counselors or HRD staff if the employee feels sexually harassed.
Managers and supervisors are held accountable by enforcing standards of appropriate office behavior and are expected to take prompt action to investigate and take appropriate action to remedy any conduct identified as sexual harassment under this policy. Employees who believe they have been subjected to sexual harassment must contact the Employee Relations Branch (ERB) on (301) 763-3701 or the Employee Assistance Program Coordinators on (301) 763-1681. All employees have an affirmative duty to report incidents or reports of Sexual Harassment to the next level supervisor. That is when sexual harassment occurs one cannot keep it secret it must be reported to the appropriate manager or office.
In addition, all employees may initiate a discrimination complaint by contacting the EEO Office on (301) 763-2853, then select 1 or 1 (800) 872-6096, then select 1, within 45 calendar days of the alleged harassment.
Employees who are in a bargaining unit position may file a complaint through the negotiated grievance procedures by contacting a union steward or official.

title: Available Relief
content:
Victims of sexual harassment have several means of redress, namely:
- Seek help from their supervisor or higher-level official.
- Report to Employee Relations Office, HRD.
- Initiate a discrimination complaint by contacting an EEO Counselor or the Department of Commerce (DOC)/Optical Character Recognition (OCR) within 45 calendar days of the harassment.
- Report the incident to the DOC Office of Inspector General.
- Report the incident as a prohibited personnel practice to the Office of Special Counsel.

title: Census Bureau Policy Statement
content: Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation violates Census Bureau policy, and it will not be tolerated. Retaliation for raising concerns of sexual orientation discrimination is also prohibited.

title: EEOC Guidelines
content:
Recent EEOC rulings make discrimination based on sexual orientation a violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and it is also prohibited under Executive Order 11478 as amended May 28, 1998. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is treating employees or applicants for employment differently from similarly situated coworkers or applicants because of:
- Their sexual orientation, sexual identity, or perceived sexual orientation.
- Their relationship with individual(s) of a particular sexual orientation, or identity.
- Their affiliation with a group that is associated with sexual orientation issues or whose membership is composed mainly of people of a particular sexual orientation(s), including an employee organization.

title: Available Relief
content:
An employee who feels that they have been subjected to discrimination based on sexual orientation has several avenues of redress, depending upon the act or decision being challenged. In general, if other jurisdictional requirements are met, an employee may follow any of these procedures:
- Informal resolution through EEO counseling and mediation.
- Office of Special Counsel complaint.
- DOC Administrative Grievance Procedure.
Depending upon the procedure, time limits for filing complaints vary. Consult an EEO Counselor for requirements and full employee rights.

title: Genetic Discrimination
content:
## Census Bureau Policy Statement
Employment discrimination based on Genetics violates Census Bureau policy, and it will not be tolerated. Retaliation for raising concerns for Genetic Discrimination is also prohibited.

title: EEO Guidelines
content:
The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (GINA) became effective on November 21, 2009. The new law prohibits employers, including federal agencies, from discrimination against job applicants and employees based on genetic information. GINA also restricts employers' acquisition and disclosure of genetic information to some very narrow circumstances, such as when it is necessary to support an employee's Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) request to care for a family member.
Genetic information includes information about an individual's genetic tests and the genetic test results of an individual's family members, as well as information about any disease, disorder, or condition of an individual's family members (i.e., an individual's family medical history). It also includes testing to determine whether someone is at an increased risk of acquiring a disease or disorder in the future.
Family medical history is included in the definition of genetic information because it is often used to determine whether someone has an increased risk of getting a disease, disorder, or condition in the future. GINA also protects individuals from employment discrimination based on the possibility of future impairments as demonstrated by their genetic information.

title: Available Relief
content:
An employer may not use genetic information in making employment decisions under any circumstances. An applicant or employee who believes that he/she has been discriminated or retaliated against based on his/her genetic information in the context of an unlawful employment practice based on Title II of the Act may access the EEO complaints process. To initiate this process, applicants and employees should contact their respective EEO offices within 45 days of an alleged discriminatory event:
U.S. Census Bureau
EEO Officer (301)763-2853
Employees and managers who have questions are also encouraged to contact their servicing Office of Civil Rights. To learn more about GINA, please visit the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's website at: [<http://www.eeoc.gov/laws/types/genetic.cfm>.]{.underline}

title: Religious Discrimination and Accommodations
content:
## Census Bureau Policy
The Census Bureau supports the provision in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act with regards to Religious Discrimination. Employees are forbidden from discriminating against fellow employees based on their religion.

title: EEOC Guidance
content: Religious discrimination involves treating a person (an applicant or employee) unfavorably because of his or her religious beliefs. The law protects not only people who belong to traditional, organized religions, such as Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism, but also others who have sincerely held religious, ethical, or moral beliefs. Religious discrimination can also involve treating someone differently because that person is married to (or associated with) an individual of a particular religion.

title: Religious Discrimination & Work Situations
content: The law forbids discrimination when it comes to any aspect of employment, including hiring, firing, pay, job assignments, promotions, layoff, training, fringe benefits, and any other term or condition of employment.

title: Religious Discrimination & Harassment
content: It is illegal to harass a person because of his or her religion. Harassment can include, for example, offensive remarks about a person\'s religious beliefs or practices. Although the law doesn\'t prohibit simple teasing, offhand comments, or isolated incidents that aren\'t very serious, harassment is illegal when it is so frequent or severe that it creates a hostile or offensive work environment or when it results in an adverse employment decision (such as the victim being fired or demoted). The harasser can be the victim\'s supervisor, a supervisor in another area, a co-worker, or someone who is not an employee of the employer, such as a client or customer.

title: Religious Discrimination and Segregation
content: Title VII also prohibits workplace or job segregation based on religion (including religious garb and grooming practices), such as assigning an employee to a non-customer contact position because of actual or feared customer preference.

title: Religious Discrimination & Reasonable Accommodation
content: The law requires an [[employer or other covered entity]{.underline}](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/coverage-0) to reasonably accommodate an employee\'s religious beliefs or practices, unless doing so would cause more than a minimal burden on the operations of the employer\'s business. This means an employer may be required to make reasonable adjustments to the work environment that will allow an employee to practice his or her religion. Examples of some common religious accommodations include flexible scheduling, voluntary shift substitutions or swaps, job reassignments, and modifications to workplace policies or practices.

title: Religious Accommodation, Dress, and Grooming Policies
content:
Unless it would be an undue hardship on the employer\'s operation of its business, an employer must reasonably accommodate an employee\'s religious beliefs or practices. This applies not only to schedule changes or leave for religious observances, but also to such things as dress or grooming practices that an employee has for religious reasons. These might include, for example, wearing head coverings or other religious dress (such as a Jewish yarmulke or a Muslim headscarf), or wearing certain hairstyles or facial hair (such as Rastafarian dreadlocks or Sikh uncut hair and beard). It also includes an employee\'s observance of a religious prohibition against wearing certain garments (such as pants or miniskirts).
When an employee or applicant needs a dress or grooming accommodation for religious reasons, he should notify the employer that he needs such an accommodation for religious reasons. If the employer reasonably needs more information, the employer and the employee should engage in an interactive process to discuss the request. If it would not pose an undue hardship, the employer must grant the accommodation.

title: Religious Discrimination, Reasonable Accommodation, and Undue Hardship
content: An employer does not have to accommodate an employee\'s religious beliefs or practices if doing so would cause undue hardship to the employer. An accommodation may cause undue hardship if it is costly, compromises workplace safety, decreases workplace efficiency, infringes on the rights of other employees, or requires other employees to do more than their share of potentially hazardous or burdensome work.

title: Religious Discrimination and Employment Policies/Practices
content: An employee cannot be forced to participate (or not participate) in a religious activity as a condition of employment.

title: Means of Resolution
content: An employee who feels that they have been subjected to discrimination based on religion may contact the EEO Office. Informal resolution through EEO counseling and Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR).

title: Employment of People with Disabilities
content:
The Census Bureau supports the hiring, placement, advancement, and retention of qualified individuals with Disabilities. RDs are encouraged to always keep in mind what the individual can do. Persons with disabilities want to be treated the same as everyone else and to compete on equal terms. This means equal responsibility as well as equal opportunity for promotion.
Disability discrimination occurs when an [employer or other entity covered](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/coverage-0) by the Americans with Disabilities Act, as amended, or the Rehabilitation Act, as amended, treats a qualified individual who is an employee or applicant unfavorably because he or she has a disability.
Disability discrimination also occurs when a covered employer or other entity treats an applicant or employee less favorably because he or she has a history of a disability (such as a past major depressive episode) or because he or she is believed to have a physical or mental impairment that is not transitory (lasting or expected to last six months or less) and minor (even if he or she does not have such an impairment).
The law requires an employer to provide RA to an employee or job applicant with a disability, unless doing so would cause significant difficulty or expense for the employer (undue hardship).
The law also protects people from discrimination based on their relationship with a person with a disability (even if they do not themselves have a disability). For example, it is illegal to discriminate against an employee because her husband has a disability.
*Note: Federal employees and applicants are covered by the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, instead of the Americans with Disabilities Act. The protections are the same.*

title: Disability Discrimination and Work Situations
content: The law forbids discrimination when it comes to any aspect of employment, including hiring, firing, pay, job assignments, promotions, layoff, training, fringe benefits, and any other term or condition of employment.

title: Disability Discrimination and Harassment
content:
It is illegal to harass an applicant or employee because he or she has a disability, had a disability in the past, or is believed to have a physical or mental impairment that is not transitory (lasting or expected to last six months or less) and minor (even if he or she does not have such an impairment).
Harassment can include, for example, offensive remarks about a person\'s disability. Although the law doesn\'t prohibit simple teasing, offhand comments, or isolated incidents that aren\'t very serious, harassment is illegal when it is so frequent or severe that it creates a hostile or offensive work environment or when it results in an adverse employment decision (such as the victim being fired or demoted).
The harasser can be the victim\'s supervisor, a supervisor in another area, a co-worker, or someone who is not an employee of the employer, such as a client or customer.

title: Disability Discrimination and Reasonable Accommodation
content:
The law requires an employer to provide reasonable accommodations to employees and job applicants with a disability, unless doing so would cause significant difficulty or expense for the employer.
A reasonable accommodation is any change in the work environment (or in the way things are usually done) to help a person with a disability apply for a job, perform the duties of a job, or enjoy the benefits and privileges of employment.
Reasonable accommodation might include, for example, making the workplace accessible for wheelchair users or providing a reader or interpreter for someone who is blind or hearing impaired.
While the federal anti-discrimination laws don\'t require an employer to accommodate an employee because he or she must care for a family member with a disability, the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA may require an employer to take such steps. The Department of Labor enforces the FMLA. For more information, call: 1 (866) 487-9243.

title: Disability Discrimination & Reasonable Accommodation & Undue Hardship
content:
An employer doesn\'t have to provide an accommodation if doing so would cause undue hardship to the employer.
Undue hardship means that the accommodation would be too difficult or too expensive to provide, considering the employer\'s size, financial resources, and the needs of the business. An employer may not refuse to provide an accommodation just because it involves some cost. An employer does not have to provide the exact accommodation the employee or job applicant wants. If more than one accommodation works, the employer may choose which one to provide.

title: Definition Of Disability
content:
Not everyone with a medical condition is protected from discrimination. To be protected, a person must be qualified for the job and have a disability as defined by the law.
A person can show that he or she has a disability in one of three ways:
- A person has a disability if he or she has a physical or mental condition that substantially limits a major life activity (such as walking, talking, seeing, hearing, or learning, or operation of a major bodily function).
- A person has a disability if he or she has a history of a disability (such as cancer that is in remission).
- A person has a disability if he or she is subject to an adverse employment action and is believed to have a physical or mental impairment that is not transitory (lasting or expected to last six months or less) and minor (even if he or she does not have such an impairment).

title: Disability-Related Questions, Medical Exams During Employment Application, and Interview Stage
content:
The law places strict limits on employers when it comes to asking any job applicants to answer disability-related questions, take a medical exam, or identify a disability.
For example, an employer may not ask a job applicant to answer disability-related questions or take a medical exam before extending a job offer. An employer also may not ask job applicants if they have a disability (or about the nature of an obvious disability). An employer may ask job applicants whether they can perform the job and how they would perform the job, with or without a reasonable accommodation.

title: Disability-Related Questions and Medical Exams After a Job Offer for Employment
content: After a job is offered to an applicant, the law allows an employer to condition the job offer on the applicant answering certain disability-related questions or successfully passing a medical exam, but only if all new employees in the same type of job must answer the questions or take the exam.

title: Disability-Related Questions & Medical Exams for Persons Who Have Started Working as Employees
content:
Once any employee is hired and has started work, an employer generally can only ask disability-related questions or require a medical exam if the employer needs medical documentation to support an employee\'s request for an accommodation or if the employer believes that an employee is not able to perform a job successfully or safely because of a medical condition.
The law also requires that employers keep all medical records and information confidential and in separate medical files.

title: EEO Complaints Guidelines and Filing Procedures
content:
## EEO Complaints
If an applicant or employee believes that they have been discriminated against by the Census Bureau when applying for a job or on the job in the terms or conditions of employment because of race, color, sex, religion, national origin, sexual orientation, age, GINA, disability, or reprisal, they must contact and EEO Counselor to file a complaint of discrimination with the Census Bureau's EEO Office. All SCO employees must fully cooperate with the EEO complaint process. RDs should ensure the full cooperation of all employees with the DOC's EEO staff, and the Census Bureau's EEO Officer, Counselors and staff in the processing and resolution of pre-complaint matters and complaints. During appeals, they must cooperate with the EEOC including routine access to SCO personnel records when required in the investigation process of the EEO complaint. Employees are subject to disciplinary action for failure to cooperate with the EEO complaint process.

title: Complaint Procedures
content: The following procedures are in accordance with the EEOC regulations, effective November 9, 1999, for the processing of federal sector complaints of discrimination.

title: Pre-Complaint
content:
## Counseling
The aggrieved must first consult with an EEO Counselor within 45 calendar days of the alleged discriminatory act or of the effective date of a personnel action before filing a formal complaint of discrimination or reprisal.
The EEO Counselor has 30 calendar days to inquire into the facts and attempt resolution. This 30-day counseling period may be extended up to an additional 60 days if the aggrieved person and the RO agree to such an extension in writing

title: Filing a Formal Complaint
content: All formal complaints must be in writing and submitted to the Census Bureau EEO Office within 15 calendar days from the receipt date of the written notice of right to file a complaint of discrimination. The EEO Office will forward the formal complaints to the DOC/OCR.

title: Acceptance or Rejection of Complaint
content: The DOC/OCR makes the decision to accept or reject a formal complaint. Accepted complaints will be assigned to an investigator. If the complaint is rejected, the complainant is notified in writing of the right to appeal to the EEOC, Office of Federal Operations (OFO), within 30 days of receipt of rejection.

title: Investigation
content:
The DOC/OCR investigation must be conducted within 180 calendar days of the filing of the complaint. This period may be extended up to 90 calendar days by written agreement between the complainant and the Census Bureau. Within the 180- day investigation period, the DOC/OCR will notify the complainant that the investigation has been completed and provide the complainant with a copy of the investigative file.
The complainant has 30 calendar days from receipt of the investigative file to request a hearing from an EEOC administrative judge; otherwise, the DOC will issue a final decision.
The complainant may request a hearing at any time after 180 calendar days from the filing of the complaint should the DOC/OCR fail to provide notice of completion of investigation.

title: Hearing and Decision
content: An EEOC administrative judge conducts the hearing and will notify the complainant and the DOC of the time and place. The EEOC administrative judge hears relevant testimony and considers documentary evidence about the allegations including the investigative report. Witnesses give testimony under oath or affirmation and can be cross-examined. Within 180 calendar days of the EEOC's receipt of a hearing request, the EEOC administrative judge will issue findings of fact and conclusions of law to the complainant and the DOC/OCR.

title: Decision
content: Within 15 calendar days of receipt of the administrative judge's decision, the agency will issue a final order notifying the complainant whether it will fully implement the administrative judge's decision. If the agency does not fully implement the administrative judge's decision it must file an appeal with the Office of Federal Operations simultaneously with issuing the agency's final order.

title: Appealing the Final Decision to EEOC
content: The complainant may appeal an agency's final action to the EEOC's Office of Federal Operations within 30 calendar days of receipt of that decision. Supporting statements must be submitted within 30 calendar days thereafter.

title: Employee's Rights
content:
## Representation
A complainant has the right to be represented by a person of his/her choice at any step of the complaint process. Reasonable attorney\'s fees and costs may be recovered, except in age discrimination complaints. Only the fees of licensed attorneys are eligible. Fees charged by lay representatives will not be recovered.
The Complainant also has the right to remain anonymous during the pre-complaint stage and the EEO Counselor may not reveal the Complainants identity to management although processing the complaint may prove to be somewhat difficult. The Complainant may waive the right to remain anonymous. If the Complainant chooses to file a formal Complaint, then he or she may not remain anonymous in the formal stage of the complaint.

title: Freedom from Reprisal
content: Complainants have the right to be free from restraint, interference, coercion, discrimination, or reprisal. A complaint of reprisal may be filed. It is filed and processed in the same manner as discrimination complaints.

title: Right to File Civil Action
content:
Except in age discrimination cases, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, authorizes a complainant to file a civil suit in an appropriate U.S. District Court. Specific time limits are:
- 90 calendar days within receipt of a final agency's order.
- 180 calendar days after filing the complaint with the agency and the agency did not issue a final agency decision.
- Within 90 calendar days of receipt of an EEOC decision.
- After 180 calendar days from the date of filing an appeal with EEOC and no EEO decision.

content: The Regional Directors (RDs), Special Census Manager and Administrative Specialist, are responsible for maintaining the minority statistics records and reporting system, which shows the effectiveness of the EEO Program within the Census Bureau. They must ensure at the time of appointment, all RCC appointees complete a Form SF-181, *Race and National Origin Identification*, and a Form SF-256, *Self-Identification of Handicap*, and the information is transferred accurately. (See Chapter 4, *Personnel Administration*, of this manual, for details concerning these forms.)

title: Recordkeeping
content:
The official EEO complaint file is maintained at the DOC/Decennial Office of Civil Rights. A copy is retained in the EEO Office, Headquarters.
The regulations require the RD to retain all records (including scratch notes) pertaining to a complaint until notified by the EEO Office that all litigation has concluded, and the case is closed.
The investigation may require you and other employees of your organization to furnish affidavits regarding matters pertaining to this complaint and to provide access to Census Bureau files and records to answer the complaint. The investigation may require records of employees holding a position like complainants in the same or different branch or division.

title: Correspondence
content:
Retain all EEO correspondence, documents, records, or memoranda as directed by OPM files retention policies and as directed by the EEO Office and/or DOC Office of Civil Rights.

title: Payroll Administration
content:
This chapter provides an overview of how Special Census employees are paid, explains allowable reimbursable expenses and how to review staff payrolls.
In addition, this chapter addresses payroll processing procedures for employees paid under the payroll system managed by the National Finance Center (NFC). The extent of processing NFC payrolls is limited to the Web Time and Attendance (GovTA) program. Preparation of payroll is administered by employees or timekeepers and certified by supervisors.
Depending on RO guidelines, some of these activities may be performed in the Special Census Office or in the Regional Office. Regardless of which office conducts the activities, the procedures remain the same.

title: Overview
content:
## Special Census Supervisor Responsibilities
The Special Census Supervisor is responsible for the administration of all payroll-related activities. Some of these duties may be delegated to Field Managers or clerks, if authorized by the RO.

title: SC-13, Budget Allocation
content: The SC-13, *Budget Allocation*, is completed by Special Census HQ staff and serves as the Special Census budget authorization. An example of Form SC-13 is shown in Illustration 6.1. This form is prepared prior to opening the SCO and should be used to monitor expenditures against the allocated Special Census budget. The RO also uses the SC-13 to monitor the SCO's expenditures.

title: The Special Census Project Number
content:
The Census Headquarters (HQ) assigns a project code to each Special Census to track supervisory payroll and other charges.
The Special Census project code is shown in Item D of the heading, on Form SC-13, *Budget Allocation*.
Figure 4. Example of Form SC-13, Budget Allocation (Not real cost data; for illustration only)

title: Staff Hours and Pay Guidelines
content:
## The Special Census Supervisor Pay
The Special Census Supervisor wages, travel, and per diem, if authorized, are charged directly to the Special Census project code and submitted to the Regional Office (RO) for processing. The RO will provide the guidelines to the Special Census Supervisor for submitting his or her payroll and expenses to the RO.

title: Special Census Office and Field Staff
content: Apart from the Special Census Supervisor, all Special Census staff are intermittent employees. They are Schedule A, temporary employees with an intermittent work schedule.

title: Intermittent Field Employees
content:
Intermittent field employees include the following positions:
- Field Supervisor
- Field Representative
Intermittent field employees are paid on a biweekly pay cycle. Every Special Census week begins at 12:01 a.m. Sunday and ends midnight on the following Saturday.
Field employees do not have a regularly scheduled tour of duty and do not earn annual or sick leave. Field employees are not allowed to work overtime hours without prior written approval from the supervisor. If overtime is necessary, the RO must approve the overtime hours before they can be worked. If a field employee works overtime without supervisory approval, they will be subject to termination. See Topic 3 for more information about the Special Census overtime policy. 180-Day FRs will not have census email accounts, they will not receive email notification of approved OT requests, or similar requests, Therefore, notification of approval or denial of OT must be a manual process. They may have to use their personal email accounts to send documents to the SCO or RO, providing they are not emailing PII information.
Field employees use the BC-27A, *Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses* and the BC-27, *Time, Attendance, and Cost Report* to record their hours, mileage, telephone, and miscellaneous expenses daily as work is completed or as reimbursable expenses are incurred. The entries made on the fillable BC-27A and BC-27 for intermittent employees are emailed to the Regional Office no later than Monday of Week 1 for the previous payroll week. RO Admin staff will key the data from the timesheet into GovTA. The Special Census Supervisor is responsible for reviewing and certifying all field employee payrolls.
Official overnight travel must be approved by a supervisor and must use the E2 travel system.

title: Intermittent Office Employees
content:
Clerks are intermittent office employees.
Intermittent office employees, like intermittent field employees, are paid on a biweekly pay cycle. Each week begins at 12:01 a.m., Sunday and ends midnight on the following Saturday. If an office employee works more than five consecutive hours in any day, they must take an unpaid meal period of 30 minutes.
Office staff will be assigned a work schedule by their supervisor. They are expected to work these hours, which should be no more than 8 hours in a day. Unlike intermittent field employees, office employees are not allowed to work more than 8 hours in a day because they have a scheduled tour of duty. If overtime is necessary, the RO will approve the overtime hours before they can be worked. If an office employee works overtime without supervisory approval, they will be subject to termination. See Topic 3 for more information about the Special Census overtime policy.
Office employees will use GovTA to record their hours by Thursday of the 2nd week of the current pay period. The following day, which is on Friday, employees may make changes or additional entries in GovTA and validate it for affirmation on the accuracy of the information.
Mileage, telephone, and miscellaneous expenses will be entered into E2 for reimbursement.

title: Paying the Staff
content: The pay rates for locally hired special census employees is determined for the geographic area in which the Special Census is being conducted. The applicable pay rates for the various positions (Field Representative, Field Supervisor, clerk, etc.) within the Special Census area are shown in Item 7 on the SC-13, *Budget Allocation (*See Illustration 6.1 on page 6-3).

title: Field Staff Pay
content:
Field Supervisors and Field Representatives are paid the regular hourly rate as specified on the SC-13. Field staff who use public transportation or use an automobile for enumeration are also reimbursed for fares paid or miles driven, as appropriate, while on official business.
Field staff are also entitled to claim the time spent traveling to and from their home to their assignment area while working. Field staff are also entitled to claim the time spent traveling to and from training sessions and for the time spent in training.

title: Office Staff Pay
content:
Clerks are paid the regular hourly rate as specified on the SC-13.
Intermittent office employees are not paid for travel miles nor travel time to the office because their duty station is the Special Census office. This is unlike field employees, whose duty stations are their homes.

title: Authorized Work Time
content:
Office supervisors inform intermittent office workers of the hours and days they are to report for duty. SCO office work schedules are established by the SCO Supervisor in consultation with the RO.
Intermittent field employees are expected to work the most productive hours for the Special Census area. Usually, this means late afternoon and evening hours during the week and daytime hours on the weekend.
Full time employees have a scheduled tour of duty. This means they report to work each day at a scheduled time.
All intermittent field employees are paid for time spent:
- Training in the classroom and on-the-job training
- Traveling to and from the training site
- Traveling on official business
- Completing work assignments
- Reviewing work assignments
- Meeting and discussing work with supervisors

title: Unauthorized Time
content:
Payment will **not** be made to intermittent employees for:
- Time used for meal periods
- Time spent running personal errands or any other non-Special Census business during the workday

title: Night Differential Hours
content:
Night differential pay is **not** authorized for Special Census employees. Under **no circumstances** will local intermittent employees be authorized night differential pay.
As the Special Census Supervisor, do not perform any of the following activities after 6 PM, without the RO's advance approval:
- Interviewing job applicants or conducting interviews with respondents.
- Preparing Field Representative materials for assignment.
- Reviewing manuals or instructional memoranda.
- Making travel arrangements.
- Transcribing data, editing, and other clerical duties.

title: Overtime Policies
content:
## Overview
Overtime will be paid to the staff only if authorized or approved by the Regional Director (or designee). If staff overtime is needed, **the Special Census Supervisor must** discuss the situation with the Regional Office. The RO will determine whether overtime will be approved.
All employees sign a Temporary Excepted Service Agreement and an Overtime Policy Agreement at the time of hiring. Their signature indicates they agree to abide by the regulations stated on the form(s). These agreements state that employees are **NOT** allowed to work overtime unless the employee receives prior approval from their supervisor.

title: Overtime Policy for SCO Field Intermittent Employees
content:
To be most effective and complete the operation on time, employees are expected to work most days in the weekly pay period. However, they must not work more than 40 hours or eight hours in a day in any weekly pay period, unless they are specifically authorized to do so in advance. Employees are expected to complete their assignments without having to work overtime. If employees feel they have more work than they can complete in a 40-hour week, they are instructed to contact their supervisor to discuss the situation. It may be that the work can be redistributed to others within the team or can otherwise be completed without needing to work overtime.
**Working overtime of more than 40 hours in a week or eight hours in a day, is not permitted without written approval from their supervisor**. If the supervisor decides that overtime hours should be authorized, then the supervisor will seek authorization from the appropriate manager or designee and let the employee know if the overtime hours can be worked. Unless you receive explicit directions from your supervisor to work overtime hours, you may not do so.

title: Unavoidable Circumstances
content:
If a field employee works more than 40 hours in a week or eight hours in a day without supervisory approval, he or she is subject to termination unless the overtime was caused by unavoidable circumstances.
Unavoidable circumstances are defined as unforeseeable circumstances beyond the employee's control. Unavoidable circumstances included but are not limited to weather-related incidents such as a blizzard, flood, hurricane, etc. Traffic is not considered an unavoidable circumstance unless a field employee is involved in an accident, delayed by an accident or unforeseen road condition.

title: Accumulating Hours
content:
Field employees are not allowed to manipulate or record hours on their timesheets on days that they were not worked. This means they must not work, for example, 42 hours in one week and record only 40 hours on the payroll forms for that week, and then record the remaining two hours on a payroll form during a subsequent week when they have worked fewer than 40 hours.
This is a manipulation of hours and is grounds for termination of employment.
If the Bureau finds that a supervisor approves or instructs an employee to manipulate or accumulate hours or otherwise submit incorrect payroll forms, then the supervisor will be terminated, and the employee who manipulated the hours may be terminated. Accumulating hours will not be tolerated.
If employees become aware of other employees accumulating hours or any supervisor giving instructions to crews to accumulate hours or to work overtime without compensation, employees must report the incident immediately to their supervisor or the Special Census Supervisor. If needed, the incident can also be reported to the RO Manager.
All employees signed a Temporary Excepted Service Agreement and an Overtime Policy Agreement at the time of hiring in which they agree to abide by the regulations on these forms.

title: Overtime Policy for Intermittent Office Employees
content:
Overtime is defined as working more than 8 hours a day or 40 hours a week, scheduled and approved in advance.
The appropriate manager or designee must approve all requests for overtime hours in advance before intermittent office employees begin working the additional hours. If they work overtime without supervisory approval, they will be subject to termination.
By signing the Temporary Excepted Service Agreement and Overtime Policy Agreement at the time of hiring, all employees agree to abide by the regulations stated on these forms.

title: Procedures for Documenting Request for Approval of Overtime Hours {#procedures-for-documenting-request-for-approval-of-overtime-hours .unnumbered}
content:
Supervisors requesting overtime must justify in writing, the need for the overtime on a CD-81, *Authorization for Paid Overtime and/or Holiday Work, and for Compensatory Overtime*.
Office employees request and obtain approval for premium pay through GovTA.
There is no need for a CD-81 if the post approval is in GovTA.
However, due to the nature of field work and following RO policy, field supervisors may obtain verbal approval from their supervisors and then follow-up with the written approval from the appropriate manager on the CD-81 form.
**Note:** When the dates for the authorized official's signature at the bottom of the CD-81 are later than the date the overtime request was verbally approved, note in Item 11 the date verbal approval was given. See illustration 6.2 for an example note.
If the request involves multiple employees, the SCS may prepare a list of employee names by Field Supervisor District and attach it to the CD-81.
Complete the CD-81 and route the documents for signature to the appropriate RO manager. In some regions, this may be the Special Census Supervisor. Follow your regional office policy.
Any list of employee names attached to the CD-81 must contain the following for each employee:
- Name
- Title
- Pay rate
- Total number of overtime hours worked
- Estimated cost
Complete the hours and estimated cost fields at the time the CD-81 is prepared for that workweek. For each week that overtime is worked, prepare a CD-81, attach the list of employees with required information, and route for appropriate signatures.
Provide a signed copy of the CD-81 to the payroll section so the clerks can use it when auditing the timesheets. Retain the original CD-81 in a permanent file marked CD-81, *Authorization for Paid Overtime and/or Holiday Work, And for Compensatory Overtime*

title: Collecting, Certifying and Reviewing Field Staff BC-27A and BC-27 Payroll Documents
content:
Special Census Field Supervisors (FS) and Field Representatives (FR) record their hours worked on a fillable pdf version of the BC-27, *Time, Attendance, and Cost Report* and miles driven (field staff only) daily on the BC-27A, *Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses*. See []{.mark}Appendix B for how to complete the BC-27 and BC-27A.
The FR/FS emails their completed timesheet to RO Admin who keys the data into GovTA.
Special Census Supervisors review the BC-27 and BC-27A bi-weekly for the FR staff. The SC supervisors must review and ensure that all entries are complete and accurate and reflect the amount of work performed.

title: Review the payroll documents
content:
The Special Census Office Manager will review the FR, FS and office employees' Clerk's hours in GovTA and certify the T&A once the timekeeper notifies the supervisor to certify.
The Special Census Office Clerks will be responsible for entering and validating their own T&A each pay period and submitting the appropriate supporting documentation to the Timekeeper as soon as the T&A record is validated. The T&A record must be validated by close-of business on the second Friday in the pay period.

title: Verify FR employee identification items -- BC-27, Time, Attendance, and Cost Report
content: SC Supervisors verify the Identification Items 1 through 6 on the payroll document. Ensure that the full name, employee ID and FR code are entered. Verify that the day of the week corresponds to the correct date.

title: Training Hours
content: Employees are paid their regular hourly rate for time spent in classroom training and on-the job-training. This includes the time spent completing appointment documents and travel to and from the training site. If training was approved for more than 8 hours in a day, including the travel time home after the training session, the employee is entitled to claim overtime for those hours.

title: Verify work hours and daily expenses
content: SC Supervisors verify that the hours and expenses claimed by Field Representatives are reasonable in relation to the assignment, and that the times of day worked are accurately reflected in the number of hours recorded.

title: Verify per diem expenses - BC-27A, Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses
content:
Per diem expenses must be approved in advance. If approved, per diem expenses for overnight travel are claimed by a field employee, through E-Gov Travel Service 2 (E2). E2 automates and consolidates the Federal travel process in a self-service Web-centric environment, covering all aspects of official travel, including travel planning, authorization, reservations, ticketing, expense reimbursement, and travel management reporting. All Schedule A employees who travel via common carrier (plane, train, or bus) must be processed in the E2 travel system. The travel arranger in the RO or SCO must create a Traveler Profile in E2 for each traveler and before a travel authorization can be created. A request to initialize a traveler in E2, so that a profile can be created is submitted in Remedy. Verify mileage claims - BC-27A, Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses
SC Supervisors review the mileage claimed by Field Representatives (FRs) and determine whether the miles driven are reasonable for the number of hours worked, the amount of work completed, and the geographic territory within the AA.
SC Supervisors should be familiar with each assignment area so they can determine what a reasonable mileage claim is. Field Supervisors should question claims for excessive mileage but relatively few hours worked. If the employee works in a sparsely populated area, it may be likely to have relatively large mileage claims in comparison to work hours.
If Field Representatives claim unreasonable mileage, suggest ways the employee can decrease excessive mileage. If excessive claims continue, Field Supervisors must report the situation to their respective supervisor or the Special Census Supervisor

title: Verify Reimbursable Expenses - BC-27A, Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses
content:
Reimbursable expenses are necessary expenses that employees may incur while performing their official duties. All purchases which an employee claims as reimbursable expenses must be approved in advance by the Special Census Supervisor.
In general, employees are provided with all the materials necessary to do their jobs. The Census Bureau will reimburse employees and authorized **field** staff for the following expenses:
- Miles traveled in a privately-owned vehicle from the office to the training site or other official work destination and return.
- Road, bridge and tunnel tolls, local bus, trolley car, ferry or subway fares when conducting official Special Census activities while in the field or when traveling from the office to an official work destination and return (toll receipts must be attached to the BC-27A).
- All supervisor-authorized purchases. Purchases totaling \$5 or more must be accompanied by a receipt.
- Field employees can claim reimbursement for official Census business related telephone calls made from their personal phone that exceed the standard or basic service; or business-related telephone calls made from a prepaid wireless plan. The Census Bureau will not reimburse the employee for charges that are covered by the employee's basic service plan. The Census Bureau will not pay for the basic service plan itself, or any changes that the employee makes to the basic service plan.
Additionally, the Census Bureau has established a CAP for reimbursement of \$240/month. Use of the employee's personal phone for Census business related calls is voluntary.
The employee will submit an itemized copy of his or her telephone bill that verifies the total of reimbursable expenses that he or she enters on his or her payroll form. The employee agreed to these terms when he or she signed the SC-1129, Personal Telephone Reimbursement Policy Agreement for Special Census Staff (Appendix C).
- Parking fees if free parking is not available at the official work destination and/or parking fees for metered spaces. Parking receipts must be attached to the BC-27A.
Field workers are reimbursed for parking fees that are necessary in the performance of their duties, including parking at the SCO if they must go to the SCO and free parking is not available.
- Because the Special Census Office staff's duty location is the Special Census Office, they are not eligible for parking fee reimbursement if free parking is not available at the Special Census Office.
- Per diem for meals and lodging expenses when overnight travel is authorized.
- The Regional Office determines the Special Census Supervisor's official duty station. If the Special Census supervisor is authorized per diem, the Regional Office will provide guidance for travel and expenses.
The Census Bureau will not reimburse the Special Census Supervisor, or any of the staff, for the following expenses:
- Daily parking expenses incurred to park at the Special Census Office if the employee's official duty station is the SCO.
- The unauthorized use of rental cars and taxis.
- Mileage driven while conducting personal errands, on breaks, or other unofficial time.
- Personal telephone calls made from home or from public telephones.
- Purchases not authorized by the supervisor.
- Any purchase or expenditure (even if approved) costing more than \$5 which does not have a receipt attached to the BC-27A.
- Towing charges.
- Parking tickets.
- Gasoline, oils, antifreeze, tires, and vehicle accessories.
- Vehicle insurance premiums.

title: Approve payroll documents
content: After verifying a payroll document in its entirety, the SC supervisor indicates approval by signing and dating the fillable BC-27 and electronically signing his or her name in the space provided in Item 11, Certified by. If not already completed, the SC supervisor should have the employee electronically sign his or her name in the space above the supervisor's name.

title: Distribute payroll documents
content: ~~The employee receives the yellow copy of the BC-27 payroll document. The white copy is submitted to the office for processing, and the field supervisor (or other supervisor, as appropriate) should keep the pink copy.~~

title: SC-20, Field Supervisor's Management Record
content: Field supervisors use the SC-20, *Field Supervisor Management Record*, to track their employees' field work and time. The field supervisor records each Field Representative hours and mileage on the SC-20. Field Supervisor must update the SC-20 every time they meet with the Field Representative in their crew.

title: Distribution of the SC-20
content: The completed SC-20s are submitted to the Special Census Supervisor at the end of the operation.

title: Payroll Forms Auditing and Check-in
content:
Field Representatives use the fillable pdf version BC-27A, *Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses* and the BC-27, *Time, Attendance, and Cost Report,* to maintain a daily record of their hours worked and miles driven while on duty. When a Field Representative's work assignment is completed for the pay period it will be email to the SCO/RO for processing.
Office staff use GovTA to record their daily hours worked. SC supervisor will review and certify GovTA at the end of the pay period.
It is the SCO's responsibility to account for all bi-weekly payroll forms from all Special Census staff, both office and field. It is important that these forms are audited for completeness and accuracy. Depending on RO guidance, auditing may be conducted by the SCO staff or the RO staff.

title: Staff Payroll Check-in
content: The BC-27A, *Field Employee's Reimbursement Expenses* and the BC-27, *Time, Attendance, and Cost Report*, is shown as Illustration 6.3. The Special Census supervisor should monitor the receipt of all BC-27As and BC-27s as well as conduct a thorough review for reasonableness and accuracy. The BC-27A and BC-27 check-in occurs at the end of the Special Census operation.

title: Fraudulent Claims
content:
An employee's claims for hours and reimbursable expenses must accurately reflect the time and cost related to their official duties.
Their claim may be forfeited if they attempt to defraud the government in connection with any expense. Additionally, there are criminal provisions under which severe penalties may be imposed if they knowingly submit a fraudulent claim.

title: Auditing Intermittent Employees Payroll
content:
Depending on RO guidelines, the BC-27A and BC-27 review and audit for the Special Census staff may be performed at the SCO or the RO. Regardless of who performs the audits, the procedures are the same.
Clerks audit all BC-27A and BC-27 to ensure that they are correct. They may make corrections to an BC-27A or BC-27 if they can be made in the SCO. Types of acceptable corrections include corrections to errors in addition and information. If the SCO edits an BC-27A or BC-27, the employee must receive a copy of the corrected BC-27A or BC-27, along with an explanation of the corrections.
If BC-27A or BC27 contain errors that cannot be corrected by the audit clerk, the forms are returned to the appropriate supervisor, and possibly to the employee, for correction. This should be an infrequent occurrence since the supervisors are required to review these forms.
Clerks perform the following review activities:
- Verify totals for regular and overtime hours worked. Note that time may be claimed in whole, half or quarter hour increments only (e.g., .1 = 15 minutes, .2 = 30 minutes, .3 = 45 minutes).
- If an employee claimed overtime, check that the employee received prior approval documented on a CD-81.
Verify the totals for miles driven and other reimbursable expenses. Verify that the totals reflect the amount claimed on the BC-27A.
- Check that the employee signed and dated the BC-27.
- Check that the SC supervisor (SCS) signed and dated the form.
After the review, the clerk signs and dates the form in Item 9, *Payroll* *Office Use*.
In preparation for the next step in processing FR's BC-27A and BC-27s, the SCO or RO Timekeepers will key data from the *BC-27 Time, Attendance, and Cost Report* into GovTA on a bi-weekly basis and validate the T&A.

title: Timekeepers Responsibilities
content:
Special Census Timekeepers are responsible for entering data from the BC-27 to ensuring time and attendance (T&A) data for SC Field Representatives are, entered, recorded, and certified in the GovTA system by the payroll processing deadline.
Timekeepers are responsible for:
- Obtaining supporting documentation, if applicable.
- Creating and updating employee Timesheet Profiles.
- Ensuring T&As are keyed and validated, as required in a timely manner by the payroll processing deadline.
- Notifying the supervisor when T&As are ready to be certified.
- Discussing T&A documentation issues with the supervisor, if applicable.
- Ensuring employees are notified by the supervisor when changes are made to a T&A data.
- Keeping supervisors updated on payroll processes.
- Only the Timekeeper can initiate and validate a corrected T&A.
- Maintaining a payroll folder for employees to file supporting documentation.
- The SCO/RO will email the Earning & Leave Statement to the FR after each pay period.

title: SC Supervisors Responsibilities
content:
SC Supervisors are responsible for controlling the T&As under their supervision. This includes reviewing T&As for accuracy and completeness, then certifying the T&A record. Supervisors must take great care when certifying T&A records since the supervisor's certification authorizes pay to the employee for time worked.
SC Supervisors are responsible for:
- Familiarizing themselves with the coding/structure of the T&A record and ensuring their timekeepers/employees have adequate T&A training.
- Providing timekeepers with appropriate information necessary to complete the T&A profile and ensuring appropriate supporting documentation is retained in the employee's payroll folder.
- Ensuring approval is obtained from the Contract Claims Services, Incorporated (CCSI) prior to certifying the Occupational Workers' Compensation (OWCP) Injury Leave.
- Ensuring that the hours and reimbursements reported on the T&A Summary are true and correct before certifying the record.
- Ensuring T&As are certified for each employee under their supervision, as required, in a timely manner to enable payment within the payroll processing cycle.
- Ensuring all T&A supporting documentation is maintained/accessible for six years.
- Providing measures to ensure a level of security exists to eliminate the possibility of T&A fraud/abuse.
